econ.behavioral.behavioral-development.p.title: Progresa repartió la ayuda por sorteo, y por eso sabemos si sirvió
econ.behavioral.behavioral-development.p.hook: En 1997 México repartió un programa social echando suertes entre pueblos. Fue lo más inteligente que hizo.
econ.behavioral.behavioral-development.p.author: author-econ-behavioral-1
econ.behavioral.behavioral-development.p.body:
En 1997 el gobierno mexicano lanzó Progresa: plata en efectivo para hogares pobres, condicionada a que los niños fueran a la escuela y la familia asistiera a controles de salud. Nada de eso era nuevo. Lo nuevo fue cómo se repartió.

Como no alcanzaba para todos a la vez, el programa entró por etapas y las localidades se asignaron al azar: unas cientos empezaron de inmediato, otras esperaron. Ese sorteo convirtió un programa social en un experimento con grupo de control, algo que casi ningún gobierno acepta hacer con su propia política estrella.

Dos detalles de diseño conductual merecen atención. El dinero se le entregaba a la madre, no al jefe de hogar declarado. Y la beca crecía con el grado escolar, porque el costo de oportunidad de mandar a un hijo a la escuela en vez de al trabajo sube con la edad.

El programa sobrevivió tres cambios de gobierno y dos cambios de nombre —Oportunidades, Prospera—, y su evidencia se copió en media América Latina. Sobrevivió porque alguien podía mostrar los números.

recall.question: ¿Qué hizo Progresa que casi ningún gobierno hace con su programa estrella?
recall.answer: Asignó al azar qué localidades entraban primero, creando un grupo de control legítimo. Gracias a eso los efectos sobre matrícula y salud se pueden atribuir al programa y no a las características de los pueblos que lo recibieron.

econ.behavioral.behavioral-finance.myopi.title: Stocks beat bonds so badly that holding bonds is the puzzle
econ.behavioral.behavioral-finance.myopi.hook: Stocks beat bonds by about six points a year for a century. No sane risk aversion explains a gap that big.
econ.behavioral.behavioral-finance.myopi.author: author-econ-behavioral-1
econ.behavioral.behavioral-finance.myopi.body:
Mehra and Prescott put the number on the table in 1985: US equities had beaten bonds by roughly six percentage points a year, and no plausible risk aversion inside a standard model can justify a gap that wide. To rationalise it you need investors so frightened of risk that they would pay ridiculous sums to avoid small gambles. That is the equity premium puzzle.

Benartzi and Thaler's 1995 answer changes the question being asked. Investors are not absurdly risk-averse over a lifetime. They are loss-averse over a *short* horizon, and they keep looking. Stocks almost certainly beat bonds over thirty years and are close to a coin flip over one — so if you check your portfolio annually, and losses hurt about twice as much as gains please, equities feel bad often enough that you demand a large premium to hold them.

On their historical calibration, the evaluation period that makes stocks and bonds equally attractive is about one year. Which is roughly how often people look.
econ.behavioral.behavioral-finance.myopi.rigor:
Take the prospect-theory value function, $v(x)=x^{0.88}$ for gains and $-2.25(-x)^{0.88}$ for losses, and apply it to the return over an *evaluation period* of length $n$ rather than to terminal wealth. With $F_n$ the distribution of $n$-year real returns for an asset, define prospective utility

$$V(n)=\mathbb{E}_{F_n}\bigl[v(R)\bigr]$$

and look for the $n$ at which $V_{\text{stocks}}(n)=V_{\text{bonds}}(n)$.

Two forces move as $n$ grows. The probability that stocks show a loss over the window falls sharply — roughly one year in three at $n=1$, close to never at $n=20$. And the kink at zero only bites when a loss actually occurs. So $V_{\text{stocks}}$ climbs steeply with $n$ while $V_{\text{bonds}}$ barely moves, and the crossing sits near one year.

The sharp part is the prediction that follows: the premium an investor demands should depend on how often they *evaluate*, not on how long they hold. Loss aversion supplies the kink, myopia supplies the frequency, and the frequency is a dial that pension design can turn.

recall.question: In myopic loss aversion, what does the "myopic" part refer to?

options.text: How often the investor evaluates the portfolio
options.why: annual checking makes a thirty-year holding feel like thirty one-year gambles.

options.text: How long the investor intends to hold the asset
options.why: the model works precisely because holding period and evaluation period come apart.

options.text: Short-sightedness about the long-run average return
options.why: investors in the model know the return distribution perfectly well.

sources.title: Myopic loss aversion and the equity premium puzzle, Quarterly Journal of Economics 110(1)
sources.author: Benartzi & Thaler

econ.behavioral.behavioral-finance.sell-.title: Investors sell what is rising and keep what is falling
econ.behavioral.behavioral-finance.sell-.hook: Investors realise about 14.8% of their winning positions and 9.8% of their losing ones. The tax code says do the opposite.
econ.behavioral.behavioral-finance.sell-.author: author-econ-behavioral-1

reviewed.notes: PGR/PLR figures attributed to non-December months and December reversal (10.8% vs 12.8%) added, per Odean 1998.

econ.behavioral.behavioral-finance.sell-.body:
Terrance Odean obtained the trading records of 10,000 accounts at a discount brokerage covering 1987 to 1993 and asked one question: when somebody sells, which of their holdings do they pick?

They pick the winners. Outside December, investors realised about 14.8% of the positions sitting on a gain and about 9.8% of those sitting on a loss. A stock that is up is roughly half again as likely to be sold as one that is down.

The name is the disposition effect, and it is backwards even before you argue about returns: in the United States realised losses are deductible and realised gains are taxed, so the tax-efficient order is precisely the reverse. December is the exception: the order flips to 10.8% of gains and 12.8% of losses, when the tax deadline finally outweighs the reluctance.

Prospect theory supplies the rest. Selling a loser converts a paper loss into a real one and prices it on the steep arm of the value function. Holding on keeps it hypothetical.

recall.question: Why is the disposition effect costly quite apart from any view about returns?

options.text: US losses are deductible and gains taxable
options.why: so selling winners first inverts the tax-efficient order.

options.text: Winning stocks always keep rising
options.why: momentum is a statistical tendency, not a guarantee, and the tax argument holds either way.

options.text: It makes investors trade more often
options.why: the effect concerns which holding is sold, not how often trading happens.

sources.title: Are investors reluctant to realize their losses?, Journal of Finance 53(5)
sources.author: Terrance Odean

econ.behavioral.behavioral-game-theory.g.title: Pick a number. Closest to two-thirds of the average wins.
econ.behavioral.behavioral-game-theory.g.hook: Pick a number from 0 to 100. Closest to two-thirds of the average wins. The equilibrium is 0 and you should not play it.
econ.behavioral.behavioral-game-theory.g.author: author-econ-behavioral-1
econ.behavioral.behavioral-game-theory.g.body:
You and a hundred other people each write down a number between 0 and 100. Whoever lands closest to two-thirds of the average takes the prize.

Think before reading on. If everyone chose at random the average would be 50, so the target is 33 — write 33. But everyone else can reason that far too, and if they all write 33 the target becomes 22. And if they all see *that*, 15. Keep unravelling and the chain ends at 0, which is the unique Nash equilibrium of the game.

So: do you write 0? What would you actually write, and what does your answer assume about how many steps the other hundred people will take?

recall.question: What number should you actually write, and why is it not 0?
recall.answer: Rosemarie Nagel ran this in 1995 and almost nobody plays 0. First-round averages sit in the mid-30s, with visible spikes at 33 and 22 — one and two rounds of reasoning away from 50. Playing 0 is a best response only in a room where everyone reasons infinitely far, and no such room exists. Winning means estimating how many steps the room will take, then taking one more.

sources.title: Unraveling in guessing games: an experimental study, American Economic Review 85(5)
sources.author: Rosemarie Nagel

econ.behavioral.behavioral-game-theory.n.title: Nobody plays the equilibrium. Everybody plays the room.
econ.behavioral.behavioral-game-theory.n.hook: Game theorists who know the equilibrium of the two-thirds game perfectly well still do not play it. They are right not to.
econ.behavioral.behavioral-game-theory.n.author: author-econ-behavioral-1
econ.behavioral.behavioral-game-theory.n.body:
The two-thirds game has an awkward property: its equilibrium is 0 and almost nobody plays it, including professional game theorists who could prove it on request. That is not stupidity. Writing 0 is a best response only against a room full of people writing 0, and there has never been such a room.

Level-k models take the observation seriously. A level-0 player is a placeholder — random, or drawn to whatever is salient. A level-1 player best-responds to level-0. A level-2 best-responds to level-1. The spikes at 33 and 22 in real data are levels 1 and 2 anchored on an average of 50.

The idea travels well beyond this game. It says people run a small, bounded number of "what will they do" steps, and the number is genuinely small: one, sometimes two. Equilibrium is not what people compute. It is where things end up after enough repetition, if they end up there at all.

The models put a distribution over those levels.
econ.behavioral.behavioral-game-theory.n.rigor:
Let $a_k$ be the action of a level-$k$ player in the $p$-beauty contest, with level-0 uniform on $[0,100]$, so $\mathbb{E}[a_0]=50$. Best-responding to a room of level-$(k-1)$ players gives

$$a_k=p\,\mathbb{E}[a_{k-1}]\ \Longrightarrow\ a_k=50\,p^{\,k}.$$

With $p=2/3$: $a_1=33.3$, $a_2=22.2$, $a_3=14.8$, and $a_k\to 0$ only in the limit. Nash is level infinity, which is a strong thing to assume about strangers.

Camerer, Ho and Chong's **cognitive hierarchy** model refines this: a level-$k$ player best-responds not to level $k-1$ alone but to a normalised Poisson distribution over levels $0,\dots,k-1$ with mean $\tau$. Fitted across many games, $\tau$ lands around $1.5$ — between one and two steps for the average player.

The other standard repair is **quantal response equilibrium** (McKelvey and Palfrey, 1995). Players best-respond with noise, choosing action $j$ with probability proportional to $\exp(\lambda u_j)$, and equilibrium is a fixed point of those noisy responses. As $\lambda\to\infty$ you recover Nash; estimated $\lambda$ is always finite. Two different repairs, one shared admission: equilibrium is a limit of something people do a little of.

recall.question: In a level-k model, what does a level-2 player believe about everyone else?

options.text: That they are level 1
options.why: so a level-2 player best-responds to a room that is best-responding to random play.

options.text: That they are playing the Nash equilibrium
options.why: that belief produces the equilibrium action, which the data almost never show.

options.text: That they are also level 2
options.why: self-consistent beliefs are exactly what level-k gives up in favour of a finite chain.

sources.title: A cognitive hierarchy model of games, Quarterly Journal of Economics 119(3)
sources.author: Camerer, Ho & Chong

econ.behavioral.bounded-rationality.scis.title: Rationality has two blades, and one of them is the world
econ.behavioral.bounded-rationality.scis.hook: Simon's answer to "why are people irrational?" was that you are staring at one blade of a pair of scissors.
econ.behavioral.bounded-rationality.scis.author: author-econ-behavioral-1
econ.behavioral.bounded-rationality.scis.body:
Nobody has ever met the decision-maker in the textbook: the one who knows every option, ranks them all, takes the best. Herbert Simon spent fifty years insisting this is not a small idealisation you can wave through. It is the wrong starting point.

His replacement was *satisficing*. Search until an option clears a threshold you already call good enough, then stop looking. A firm hunts an acceptable return, not the maximum. You did not view every apartment in Bogotá before signing a lease, and you were right not to.

Simon's best image came in 1990: rational behaviour is shaped by a scissors whose two blades are the structure of the environment and the computational limits of the mind. Study one blade and you cannot explain the cut. Which is why "people are irrational" is usually the lazy diagnosis — half the time it was the environment that moved, not the mind.

recall.question: What does satisficing replace in the textbook picture of choice?

options.text: Exhaustive search for the best option
options.why: you stop at the first option that clears a good-enough threshold.

options.text: The idea that people have preferences at all
options.why: satisficing still needs preferences; it only changes how far you search.

options.text: The assumption that people dislike risk
options.why: risk attitude is a separate question from how long you keep looking.

sources.title: Herbert A. Simon — includes "Invariants of human behavior" (1990)
sources.author: Herbert A. Simon

econ.behavioral.heuristics-biases.linda-.title: Linda is a bank teller, and 85% of people got it wrong
econ.behavioral.heuristics-biases.linda-.hook: Adding a detail to a story can only make it less likely. About 85% of people bet the other way.
econ.behavioral.heuristics-biases.linda-.author: author-econ-behavioral-1
econ.behavioral.heuristics-biases.linda-.body:
Linda is thirty-one, single, outspoken, very bright. She majored in philosophy, cared deeply about discrimination and social justice, and went on anti-nuclear demonstrations. Which is more probable: that Linda is a bank teller, or that Linda is a bank teller and active in the feminist movement?

About 85% of people pick the second. It cannot be right. Every feminist bank teller is a bank teller, so the second group sits *inside* the first — adding a detail can shrink a probability, never grow it. Tversky and Kahneman published this in 1983 and named it the conjunction fallacy: we judge by how well the story fits, not by how much room the story leaves.

The honest footnote: wording matters. Ask instead "out of 100 women like Linda, how many are bank tellers? how many are feminist bank tellers?" and the error rate drops to roughly 20%. Counting helps. It does not make the fallacy vanish, and the original version is the one your head runs by default.
econ.behavioral.heuristics-biases.linda-.rigor:
Probability is monotone under inclusion. For events $A$ and $B$, write $A$ as the disjoint union $(A\cap B)\cup(A\cap B^{c})$. Since $\mathbb{P}$ is a measure,

$$\mathbb{P}(A)=\mathbb{P}(A\cap B)+\mathbb{P}(A\cap B^{c})\ \ge\ \mathbb{P}(A\cap B).$$

There is no distribution on any sample space under which "teller *and* feminist" beats "teller". The ranking people give is not a poor estimate of a probability; it is not a probability at all.

So what is it? Tversky and Kahneman's answer is **representativeness**: people substitute the similarity of Linda to a prototype for the probability of a category. Similarity is not monotone under conjunction — adding "feminist" makes the description fit *better*, so fit rises while measure falls. Judge by fit and you reproduce the observed order; judge by measure and you cannot.

The frequency rescue works because "how many out of 100" makes the nesting visible. The room the story leaves stops being an abstraction and becomes something you are literally counting.

recall.question: Why can "bank teller and feminist" never be more probable than "bank teller"?

options.text: The conjunction is a subset, and probability is monotone
options.why: $\mathbb{P}(A\cap B)\le\mathbb{P}(A)$ always.

options.text: Feminists are rare among bank tellers
options.why: the ranking would still be impossible even if almost every teller were a feminist.

options.text: The description of Linda is irrelevant
options.why: it is highly relevant; it simply cannot reverse a set inclusion.

sources.title: Extensional versus intuitive reasoning: the conjunction fallacy in probability judgment, Psychological Review 90(4)
sources.author: Tversky & Kahneman

econ.behavioral.heuristics-biases.the-ca.title: Remember Bayes? Watch what happens when the base rate goes
econ.behavioral.heuristics-biases.the-ca.hook: A witness who is right 80% of the time says the cab was blue. The cab was probably green.
econ.behavioral.heuristics-biases.the-ca.author: author-econ-behavioral-1
econ.behavioral.heuristics-biases.the-ca.body:
Remember Bayes' rule — the one that says evidence *updates* a prior instead of replacing it? Tversky and Kahneman built the cleanest demonstration that people know the rule and do not use it.

A cab hits someone at night. In that city 85% of the cabs are green and 15% are blue. A witness says the cab was blue, and tested under the same night conditions this witness gets the colour right 80% of the time. How likely is it that the cab really was blue?

Most people answer 80%. They have reported the witness's reliability and quietly dropped the fact that blue cabs are rare. The Bayesian answer is 41%: the cab was probably green, even though a reliable witness is telling you otherwise.

A base rate is not a technicality you may discard once real evidence arrives. It is half of the calculation, and here it is the bigger half. Three lines of arithmetic show why.
econ.behavioral.heuristics-biases.the-ca.rigor:
Let $B$ be "the cab was blue" and $W$ "the witness says blue". The prior is $\mathbb{P}(B)=0.15$; the likelihoods are $\mathbb{P}(W\mid B)=0.8$ and $\mathbb{P}(W\mid B^{c})=0.2$. Then

$$\mathbb{P}(B\mid W)=\frac{0.8\times 0.15}{0.8\times 0.15+0.2\times 0.85}=\frac{0.12}{0.12+0.17}\approx 0.41.$$

Read the denominator rather than the answer. Out of 100 such accidents, 12 are blue cabs correctly identified and 17 are green cabs misidentified. There are simply more green cabs available to be mistaken for blue, so an 80%-reliable witness saying "blue" is wrong more often than right.

The odds form makes the missing half visible. Prior odds $15:85$, likelihood ratio $0.8/0.2=4$, posterior odds $60:85$, which is $0.41$. The likelihood ratio is everything the evidence contributes; the prior odds are the base rate. People report the first factor and never multiply by the second — exactly the substitution the story described.

recall.question: The witness is right 80% of the time, yet the answer is 41%. Why?

options.text: There are simply more green cabs available to be mistaken
options.why: 17 green misidentifications per 100 accidents against 12 correct blue ones.

options.text: The witness is unreliable at night
options.why: the 80% figure already is the night-time accuracy.

options.text: Bayes' rule does not apply to eyewitnesses
options.why: it applies to any evidence with a known likelihood ratio.

econ.behavioral.heuristics-biases.the-wh.title: The wheel of fortune was rigged, and it moved every answer
econ.behavioral.heuristics-biases.the-wh.hook: A number produced by a rigged wheel of fortune moved people's estimates by twenty points.
econ.behavioral.heuristics-biases.the-wh.author: author-econ-behavioral-1
econ.behavioral.heuristics-biases.the-wh.body:
Tversky and Kahneman spun a wheel of fortune in front of their subjects. The wheel was rigged: it stopped on 10, or it stopped on 65. Then they asked what percentage of the countries in the United Nations are African.

The group that had watched it land on 10 answered 25, on median. The group that had watched it land on 65 answered 45. A number everyone had just seen a wheel produce — a number with exactly zero information in it — shifted estimates by twenty points.

That is anchoring, published in *Science* in 1974, and it is one of the sturdiest things in the field. When the big multi-lab replication projects went back through the classics after 2011, anchoring survived; ego depletion and several priming results did not. The uncomfortable part is not that people are influenced. It is that warning them about the anchor, or paying them for accuracy, barely helps.

recall.question: What makes the wheel-of-fortune result so unsettling?

options.text: The anchor carried no information
options.why: subjects watched a wheel produce it, and it still moved estimates by twenty points.

options.text: Subjects did not know the true answer
options.why: true but ordinary; the point is that a random number changed the guess.

options.text: People who saw the high anchor knew more geography
options.why: groups were randomly assigned, so knowledge cannot explain the gap.

sources.title: Judgment under uncertainty: heuristics and biases, Science 185(4157)
sources.author: Tversky & Kahneman

econ.behavioral.loss-aversion-endowment..title: The card dealers did not flinch, and that is the interesting part
econ.behavioral.loss-aversion-endowment..hook: The endowment effect showed up in every classroom. Then someone ran it on people who trade for a living.
econ.behavioral.loss-aversion-endowment..author: author-econ-behavioral-1
econ.behavioral.loss-aversion-endowment..body:
The mug result is famous because it is so easy to run: hand out a mug, open a market, watch almost nothing trade. John List went to sports-card conventions and ran the same design on people who buy and sell small collectibles all weekend, every weekend.

Novices behaved like the Cornell undergraduates. Experienced dealers did not. The more market experience a subject had, the closer their behaviour came to the textbook prediction — and List's follow-up experiment showed the experience was doing the work, rather than traders simply being unusual people to begin with.

Then Plott and Zeiler pushed harder in 2005: run the elicitation with full training, anonymity and practice rounds, they argued, and the gap between what sellers demand and what buyers offer can disappear entirely. That claim is contested — other groups get the gap back with careful procedures — and it is the most honest thing to say about the endowment effect today: robust in the laboratory, smaller in markets, and still argued about at the level of experimental plumbing.

recall.question: What did List's sports-card experiments add to the mug result?

options.text: Market experience shrinks the endowment effect
options.why: and his follow-up design showed the experience causes the shrinkage rather than merely accompanying it.

options.text: The endowment effect does not exist
options.why: novices in the same experiments showed it clearly.

options.text: Collectibles are special goods
options.why: the point was about the traders' experience, not the goods.

sources.title: Does market experience eliminate market anomalies?, Quarterly Journal of Economics 118(1)
sources.author: John A. List

sources.author: Plott & Zeiler

econ.behavioral.loss-aversion-endowment..title: The mug that was worth twice as much once it was yours
econ.behavioral.loss-aversion-endowment..hook: Half a Cornell class got a free mug. Minutes later the mug was worth more than twice what the other half would pay.
econ.behavioral.loss-aversion-endowment..author: lead

reviewed.notes: Buyer valuation corrected from about 3.50 to about 3 dollars (KKT 1990 medians are roughly 7 vs 3); hook now says more than twice.

econ.behavioral.loss-aversion-endowment..body:
In 1990 Kahneman, Knetsch and Thaler handed coffee mugs to half a class at random. Then they opened a market. Owners could sell, non-owners could buy, same mug, same room. Economics 101 predicts about half the mugs change hands, because ownership was random and tastes are not.

Almost none did. Sellers wanted about \$7. Buyers offered about \$3. The moment the mug was *yours*, giving it up registered as a loss, and losses hurt about twice as much as the equivalent gain feels good.

That is loss aversion, the load-bearing wall of prospect theory. It is why free trials work, why you hold losing stocks too long, and why "you'll lose \$50" moves people that "you'll save \$50" does not. The catch: the size of the effect depends on context and experience, and experienced traders show much less of it. The rigor is the function that produces the number.
econ.behavioral.loss-aversion-endowment..rigor:
Prospect theory replaces utility over wealth with a value function over *changes* from a reference point:

$$v(x)=\begin{cases} x^{\alpha} & x\ge 0\\ -\lambda(-x)^{\beta} & x<0\end{cases}$$

Tversky and Kahneman's 1992 fit gives $\alpha\approx\beta\approx0.88$ and $\lambda\approx2.25$. The exponent below one is diminishing sensitivity: the second lost dollar stings less than the first. The $\lambda$ is loss aversion — a kink at zero, where the loss arm is about 2.25 times steeper than the gain arm.

That kink is the mug. Own it, and the reference point moves to "mug in hand", so selling is coded as a loss and priced by the steep arm, while buying is coded as a gain and priced by the shallow one. Two curves, one ratio, and the gap between \$7 and \$3.

recall.question: Why do owners price the mug higher than buyers, in prospect-theory terms?

options.text: Owning moves their reference point, so selling is coded as a loss and priced on the steeper arm of the value function
options.why: the $\lambda\approx2.25$ kink.

options.text: Owners simply like mugs more
options.why: ownership was assigned at random, so tastes cannot explain the gap.

options.text: Buyers cannot afford the mug
options.why: the sums are a few dollars, and the same gap appears with tokens redeemable for cash.

econ.behavioral.mental-accounting.cab-dr.title: Cab drivers quit early on exactly the days they should stay out
econ.behavioral.mental-accounting.cab-dr.hook: On the busiest days, New York cab drivers went home early. Twenty-five years later economists are still arguing about why.
econ.behavioral.mental-accounting.cab-dr.author: author-econ-behavioral-1
econ.behavioral.mental-accounting.cab-dr.body:
Standard labour supply says work longer when the wage is high. New York taxi drivers face an hourly take that swings with rain, conventions and broken subway lines, varies enormously between days and barely at all within one — which makes them close to a natural experiment on the question.

Camerer, Babcock, Loewenstein and Thaler went through three samples of trip sheets in 1997 and found the elasticity pointing the wrong way, most sharply among inexperienced drivers: on good days they went home early. The story is a daily income target. Hit roughly the usual take, feel finished, park the cab — and on a slow day keep driving into the night to get there. The target is a reference point, and falling short of it is coded as a loss.

Treat this as a live argument rather than a settled fact. Henry Farber, working with millions of electronic trip records, gets elasticities that are usually positive. Thakral and Tô found in 2021 that income targeting survives once the reference point is allowed to drift during the day. Three teams, one question, twenty-five years.

recall.question: What makes New York cab drivers a good test of reference-dependent labour supply?

options.text: Their hourly earnings vary a lot between days and little within one
options.why: so the day's wage is close to randomly assigned.

options.text: They are paid a fixed salary
options.why: they are not, and the whole design depends on their earnings fluctuating.

options.text: They commit to their hours a year ahead
options.why: they choose when to stop each day, which is the decision being measured.

sources.title: Labor supply of New York City cabdrivers: one day at a time, Quarterly Journal of Economics 112(2)
sources.author: Camerer, Babcock, Loewenstein & Thaler

econ.behavioral.mental-accounting.the-lo.title: Lose the ticket and you go home. Lose the cash and you watch.
econ.behavioral.mental-accounting.the-lo.hook: Lose the ticket and 46% buy another. Lose an identical banknote and 88% do.
econ.behavioral.mental-accounting.the-lo.author: author-econ-behavioral-1
econ.behavioral.mental-accounting.the-lo.body:
You paid \$10 for a theatre ticket. At the door you find the ticket is gone. Would you pay \$10 again? In Tversky and Kahneman's 1981 study, 46% said yes.

Different group, different wording. You are going to the theatre, admission is \$10, paid at the door. On the way in you discover you have lost a \$10 note. Would you still buy the ticket? Here 88% said yes.

You are \$10 poorer in both worlds and the play costs the same in both. The only thing that changed is where the loss gets filed. A lost ticket goes into the account marked *this evening at the theatre*, which makes the evening cost \$20 — an absurd price for a play. A lost banknote goes into general funds, where it makes you very slightly poorer and nothing else happens.

Money is fungible. The accounts in your head are not, and they are the ones doing the deciding.

recall.question: Why do the two theatre versions get such different answers?

options.text: The lost ticket is filed in the evening's own account
options.why: a replacement makes the evening cost \$20, while a lost note only makes you poorer.

options.text: People value tickets more than cash
options.why: the ticket and the note are worth the same \$10 and both are gone.

options.text: The second group had more money
options.why: respondents were randomly assigned to the two versions of the question.

sources.title: The framing of decisions and the psychology of choice, Science 211(4481)
sources.author: Tversky & Kahneman

econ.behavioral.neuroeconomics.no-loss-c.title: The brain has no loss centre, which is stranger than having one
econ.behavioral.neuroeconomics.no-loss-c.hook: If losses hurt twice as much, there should be a pain circuit for them. There is not — and that is the finding.
econ.behavioral.neuroeconomics.no-loss-c.author: author-econ-behavioral-1
econ.behavioral.neuroeconomics.no-loss-c.body:
If losses hurt about twice as much as equivalent gains please, the tidy prediction is a dedicated circuit: some region that fires for losses and stays quiet for gains. Tom, Fox, Trepel and Poldrack went looking for it in 2007, scanning people deciding whether to accept coin-flip gambles with real money on the line.

There is no such region. The areas that track value — ventral striatum, ventromedial prefrontal cortex — raise their activity as the possible gain grows and *lower* it as the possible loss grows, in the same circuit, on the same scale. What differs is the slope. The fall per unit of loss is steeper than the rise per unit of gain, and how much steeper a given person's slopes are predicts how loss-averse that person's choices are. They called it neural loss aversion.

The complement is a blunt little experiment: De Martino, Camerer and Adolphs tested two patients whose damage was confined to the amygdala and found their loss aversion gone, with ordinary risk aversion intact.
econ.behavioral.neuroeconomics.no-loss-c.rigor:
The design is parametric rather than categorical, which is what makes the claim testable. Each trial offers a 50/50 gamble with gain $G$ and loss $L$ varied independently across a grid, and the subject accepts or rejects. Two fits run in parallel.

Behaviourally, the probability of accepting is modelled as a logistic function of $G-\lambda L$, giving each subject a choice-based loss aversion coefficient $\lambda$.

Neurally, the response in each voxel is regressed on both parameters,

$$y=\beta_0+\beta_{G}\,G+\beta_{L}\,L+\varepsilon,$$

and the quantity of interest is $\lambda_{\text{neural}}=-\beta_L/\beta_G$: the asymmetry of one circuit's sensitivity in the two directions.

The result is that $\beta_G>0$ and $\beta_L<0$ in striatal and ventromedial prefrontal regions, that no region shows a selective *increase* for growing losses, and that $\lambda_{\text{neural}}$ correlates across subjects with the behavioural $\lambda$. That correlation is what turns a picture into evidence.

Two caveats worth carrying into every scan you read. Reverse inference — reasoning backwards from a region to a mental process — is weak. And absence of activation is much weaker evidence than presence. Which is exactly why the lesion patients matter: lesions test necessity, scans only test correlation.

recall.question: What made the 2007 scan evidence rather than a pretty picture?

options.text: The neural asymmetry predicted individual behaviour
options.why: each subject's $\lambda_{\text{neural}}$ tracked their choice-based $\lambda$.

options.text: A region lit up only for losses
options.why: no such selective loss region was found, and that absence was the headline.

options.text: The sample was very large
options.why: samples of this kind are small; the parametric design and the individual correlation carried the argument.

sources.title: The neural basis of loss aversion in decision-making under risk, Science 315(5811)
sources.author: Tom, Fox, Trepel & Poldrack

econ.behavioral.nudges.el-milagro-espano.title: El milagro español de los trasplantes no fue la ley
econ.behavioral.nudges.el-milagro-espano.hook: La ley de consentimiento presunto es de 1979. Durante diez años no movió ni una cifra.
econ.behavioral.nudges.el-milagro-espano.author: author-econ-behavioral-1

reviewed.notes: The 2022 donor rate softened to more than 46 pmp: the official ONT figure is 46.03, the cited page rounds it to 47.

econ.behavioral.nudges.el-milagro-espano.body:
España lleva más de tres décadas a la cabeza del mundo en donación de órganos. La explicación fácil es la ley: desde 1979 el país tiene consentimiento presunto, es decir, usted es donante salvo que haya dicho lo contrario.

Las fechas desmienten la explicación fácil. La ley es de 1979 y durante diez años no movió nada: en 1989 España seguía en unos 14 donantes por millón de habitantes, una cifra europea del montón. Lo que cambió ese año fue la creación de la Organización Nacional de Trasplantes, con coordinadores dentro de cada hospital —casi siempre médicos de cuidados intensivos— entrenados para detectar donantes potenciales y para hablar con las familias en el peor momento de su vida. De 14 se pasó a 39,7 por millón en 2015 y a más de 46 en 2022.

La lección incomoda a los entusiastas de la arquitectura de decisiones. La casilla marcada por defecto abre la puerta; el resultado lo pusieron la logística y las conversaciones. Grecia también tiene consentimiento presunto y sigue al final de la tabla.

recall.question: ¿Por qué la ley de 1979 no explica el liderazgo español en donación de órganos?
recall.answer: Porque en diez años no movió la cifra: España seguía en unos 14 donantes por millón en 1989. El salto llegó con la ONT y sus coordinadores hospitalarios, no con el cambio de consentimiento.

econ.behavioral.nudges.how-big-is-a-nudg.title: A nudge is real, and about six times smaller than you read
econ.behavioral.nudges.how-big-is-a-nudg.hook: Same interventions, two literatures: 1.4 percentage points in government trials, 8.7 in the published papers.
econ.behavioral.nudges.how-big-is-a-nudg.author: author-econ-behavioral-1

reviewed.notes: Changed to two of the largest US nudge units, per the paper; source title now cites Econometrica 90(1). All figures verified.

econ.behavioral.nudges.how-big-is-a-nudg.body:
Two numbers from the same literature. Stefano DellaVigna and Elizabeth Linos went through 126 randomised trials run by two of the largest US nudge units — 23 million participants, every trial those units ran, whether or not anyone wrote it up. Average effect on take-up: 1.4 percentage points, an 8.1% relative improvement.

Then they looked at the academic papers testing the same kinds of intervention. Average effect: 8.7 percentage points, a 33.5% improvement. Six times bigger.

The gap is not that governments are clumsy. The authors show that publication bias, amplified by small samples, accounts for the *whole* difference: an underpowered study only clears significance when its estimate happens to be large, and those are the ones that reach print. The pattern repeated in 2022 when a PNAS meta-analysis reported a healthy average nudge effect and a reply in the same journal, correcting for publication bias, found essentially nothing left of it.

So nudges work, cheaply, at a scale worth having. And every headline effect size you have read is too big. Both sentences.

recall.question: Why are nudge-unit effects so much smaller than published academic effects?

options.text: Publication bias plus low power
options.why: a small study only reaches significance when its estimate is large, and those are the ones published.

options.text: Government trials are run badly
options.why: the nudge-unit trials are larger and preregistered; the difference is selection, not sloppiness.

options.text: Nudges stop working once the public knows about them
options.why: the comparison is across two literatures, not before and after publicity.

sources.title: RCTs to scale: comprehensive evidence from two nudge units, Econometrica 90(1) (NBER working paper 27594)
sources.author: DellaVigna & Linos

econ.behavioral.nudges.the-default-is-th.title: Austria says yes 99.98% of the time. Germany says yes 12%.
econ.behavioral.nudges.the-default-is-th.hook: Austria's effective consent to organ donation is 99.98%. Germany's is about 12%. The difference is which box is pre-ticked.
econ.behavioral.nudges.the-default-is-th.author: author-econ-behavioral-1
econ.behavioral.nudges.the-default-is-th.body:
Two neighbours, similar hospitals, similar culture, and effective consent to organ donation that differs by nearly ninety points. Austria sits at 99.98%. Germany sits at about 12%.

The difference is one line on a form. Austria presumes you consent unless you opt out; Germany asks you to opt in. Johnson and Goldstein laid the pattern out in *Science* in 2003 across a set of European countries and the split is brutally clean: opt-in countries cluster low, opt-out countries press against the ceiling. Nobody is choosing differently. The box starts in a different position.

That is what a default is — the outcome of doing nothing, in a world where doing nothing is the most popular action there is.

The honest caveat, which this literature took years to say loudly: consent on paper is not a transplant. Greece has presumed consent and one of Europe's lowest donation rates. The form is necessary. It is nowhere near sufficient.

recall.question: Why does the Austria–Germany consent gap say so little about what people want?

options.text: Almost everyone in both countries does nothing
options.why: so the number measures the pre-ticked box rather than a decision.

options.text: Austrians are more altruistic
options.why: no attitude survey between the two countries shows anything like an eighty-eight-point gap.

options.text: German forms are harder to complete
options.why: what differs is which answer requires action, not how hard the paperwork is.

econ.behavioral.overconfidence.ninety-pe.title: Write down five ranges you are 90% sure about
econ.behavioral.overconfidence.ninety-pe.hook: Five questions, five ranges, 90% confidence each. If you are calibrated you should miss half of one.
econ.behavioral.overconfidence.ninety-pe.author: author-econ-behavioral-1
econ.behavioral.overconfidence.ninety-pe.body:
A test you can score on yourself. Answer each of these with a *range*, not a number, and make the range wide enough that you are 90% confident the true value falls inside it.

The length of the Nile, in kilometres. The year Mozart was born. The number of African member states of the United Nations. The gestation of an Asian elephant, in days. The air distance from Bogotá to Madrid, in kilometres.

Five questions at 90% each: a calibrated person misses half of one. Write your ranges down before looking anything up, count your misses, and then ask what that miss rate does to a budget, a forecast, or a thesis timeline.

recall.question: How many of your five 90% ranges contained the truth?
recall.answer: Nile ≈ 6,650 km; Mozart 1756; 54 African countries; Asian elephant ≈ 640 days; Bogotá–Madrid ≈ 8,010 km. Almost nobody misses only half of one. In the classic calibration studies, people's 90% intervals contain the truth closer to 50% of the time, and warning or training them barely moves it. The repair is not knowing more. It is widening the interval until it feels embarrassing — which is roughly where honest 90% coverage begins.

econ.behavioral.overconfidence.ninety-th.title: 93% of drivers are in the better half
econ.behavioral.overconfidence.ninety-th.hook: 93% of American drivers put themselves in the better half. The effect reverses for hard skills.
econ.behavioral.overconfidence.ninety-th.author: author-econ-behavioral-1

reviewed.notes: Added Svenson (1981, Acta Psychologica) as the source for the 93% figure.

econ.behavioral.overconfidence.ninety-th.body:
Ola Svenson asked American drivers in 1981 to rank themselves against the rest of the sample. 93% placed themselves in the top half for driving skill. The same trick works for teaching quality, popularity, and — best of all — for the ability to judge oneself without bias.

What it is not is proof that people are stupid. Ask about a genuinely difficult skill, juggling or programming, and the better-than-average effect can flip into a *worse*-than-average effect. People are not uniformly vain. They are bad at knowing where the middle is.

sources.title: Are we all less risky and more skillful than our fellow drivers?, Acta Psychologica 47(2)
sources.author: Ola Svenson

econ.behavioral.prospect-theory.four-box.title: Four boxes that hold almost everything people do about risk
econ.behavioral.prospect-theory.four-box.hook: One risk attitude cannot bend twice. The fourfold pattern needs both of prospect theory's moves at once.
econ.behavioral.prospect-theory.four-box.author: author-econ-behavioral-1
econ.behavioral.prospect-theory.four-box.body:
Put the two moves together — outcomes as changes through a kinked value function, probabilities bent through an inverse S — and you get a prediction no single risk attitude can generate. Whether someone gambles depends on two things at once: gain or loss, and large probability or small.

High-probability gains: take the sure thing. High-probability losses: gamble rather than accept a certain loss. Low-probability gains: buy the lottery ticket. Low-probability losses: buy the insurance. Risk-averse, risk-seeking, risk-seeking, risk-averse, in that order. Tversky and Kahneman called it the fourfold pattern, and it is the sharpest thing the theory predicts, because one curvature parameter cannot bend twice.

The 1992 rewrite was not cosmetic either. The 1979 original could hand a higher value to a prospect that loses outcome by outcome. Ranking the outcomes first repairs it — and takes us back to the two choices that started this.
econ.behavioral.prospect-theory.four-box.rigor:
Cumulative prospect theory evaluates a prospect with outcomes $x_1<\dots<x_n$ and probabilities $p_i$ as $V=\sum_i \pi_i\,v(x_i)$, where the decision weights are *differences of the weighting function applied to cumulative probabilities*. For gains, ranked from the best downwards,

$$\pi_i=w\Bigl(\sum_{j\ge i}p_j\Bigr)-w\Bigl(\sum_{j>i}p_j\Bigr).$$

Losses are handled the same way from the worst upwards, using $\delta=0.69$ in place of $\gamma=0.61$.

Why the repair matters: in the 1979 form, applying $w$ to each $p_i$ separately gives $\sum_i w(p_i)\ne 1$, and a prospect that is stochastically dominated can come out ahead. Rank-dependent weights telescope to exactly $1$, so dominance is preserved by construction.

Now go back to episode 1. With $\gamma=0.61$, $w(1)-w(0.89)\approx 0.30$ while $w(0.11)-w(0)\approx 0.20$. The same eleven percentage points are worth half again as much when they are the last step to certainty. Feed that asymmetry into A-versus-B and C-versus-D and the Allais pair stops being a contradiction and becomes a consequence. The axiom was wrong about people, not the people about the axiom.

recall.question: What did the 1992 cumulative version fix in the 1979 original?

options.text: Weighting each probability separately could rank a dominated prospect above one that beats it
options.why: rank-dependent weights cannot.

options.text: The value function was not steep enough on the loss side
options.why: the value function was essentially unchanged; the repair was on the probability side.

options.text: It removed the reference point
options.why: reference dependence is the core of both versions and stayed put.

sources.title: Advances in prospect theory: cumulative representation of uncertainty, Journal of Risk and Uncertainty 5(4)
sources.author: Tversky & Kahneman

econ.behavioral.prospect-theory.lottery-.title: Why one person buys lottery tickets and insurance
econ.behavioral.prospect-theory.lottery-.hook: Buying insurance makes you risk-averse. Buying a lottery ticket makes you risk-seeking. Millions of people do both before lunch.
econ.behavioral.prospect-theory.lottery-.author: author-econ-behavioral-1
econ.behavioral.prospect-theory.lottery-.body:
An expected-utility maximiser who buys insurance is risk-averse. An expected-utility maximiser who buys lottery tickets is risk-seeking. Millions of people do both on the same afternoon, and they are not confused.

Prospect theory's second move explains it: probabilities enter a decision bent. A 1% chance gets treated as bigger than 1%, which is what makes both the jackpot and the house fire feel live enough to pay for. A 99% chance gets treated as smaller than 99%, which is why a near-certain good outcome still feels worth insuring, and why certainty itself commands a premium.

The bend is not an arithmetic mistake. Ask people to *estimate* a 1% risk and they do fine. Ask them to *act* on it and the weight it carries is visibly larger. The gap between the stated probability and the decision weight is the entire function.

Its shape is an inverse S, and the 1992 paper fitted it.
econ.behavioral.prospect-theory.lottery-.rigor:
In cumulative prospect theory the weight on an outcome comes from applying a function to *cumulative* probabilities, which is what keeps the model from violating stochastic dominance. Tversky and Kahneman's one-parameter form is

$$w(p)=\frac{p^{\gamma}}{\bigl(p^{\gamma}+(1-p)^{\gamma}\bigr)^{1/\gamma}},$$

with their 1992 estimates $\gamma=0.61$ for gains and $\delta=0.69$ for losses.

Read the shape off the formula. $w(0)=0$, $w(1)=1$, and in between the curve crosses the diagonal exactly once, near $p\approx 0.34$. Below the crossing $w(p)>p$: at $\gamma=0.61$ a 1% chance carries a weight of about $0.055$. Above it $w(p)<p$: a 99% chance carries about $0.91$. The function is steepest at both endpoints, which is the formal version of "certainty gets a bonus".

That endpoint steepness is precisely what episode 1 needed. Moving from 100% to 99% destroys more weight than moving from 11% to 10%, so a shared branch refuses to cancel. Bend the probabilities and the Allais contradiction turns into an ordinary preference.

One thing is still missing: how to combine bent probabilities with a kinked value function without the model predicting nonsense.

recall.question: What does an inverse-S weighting function say about a 1% chance?

options.text: It gets a decision weight larger than 1%
options.why: small probabilities are overweighted, which is why lotteries and insurance both sell.

options.text: It gets a weight of exactly 1%
options.why: that is expected utility, the model these data reject.

options.text: It gets a weight smaller than 1%
options.why: underweighting happens at the top of the range, not the bottom.

sources.title: Advances in prospect theory: cumulative representation of uncertainty, Journal of Risk and Uncertainty 5(4)
sources.author: Tversky & Kahneman

econ.behavioral.prospect-theory.two-choi.title: Two choices, and you have just broken the theory
econ.behavioral.prospect-theory.two-choi.hook: Two pairs of gambles. Almost everyone answers in a way that no utility function on earth can produce.
econ.behavioral.prospect-theory.two-choi.author: author-econ-behavioral-1
econ.behavioral.prospect-theory.two-choi.body:
Choose. **A**: one million, guaranteed. **B**: a 10% chance of five million, an 89% chance of one million, and a 1% chance of nothing.

Now choose again. **C**: an 11% chance of one million, otherwise nothing. **D**: a 10% chance of five million, otherwise nothing.

Most people take A, then take D. Maurice Allais presented this at a Paris colloquium in 1952 and published it in *Econometrica* in 1953 to make one point: those two answers cannot both come from an expected-utility maximiser. Not for any utility function. Not for any degree of risk aversion. The pair is not a taste. It is a contradiction.

You can feel where it comes from. In the first choice, B puts a 1% hole in a sure thing, and a sure thing is special. In the second there is no sure thing left to protect, so you go for the money. Certainty is collecting a bonus the axioms do not permit.

The axiom it kills has a name, and it is worth watching die.
econ.behavioral.prospect-theory.two-choi.rigor:
The casualty is the **independence axiom** of von Neumann and Morgenstern: if $L\succ L'$, then $\alpha L+(1-\alpha)M \succ \alpha L'+(1-\alpha)M$ for every lottery $M$ and every $\alpha\in(0,1]$. Mixing both sides with the same thing cannot flip a preference.

Normalise $u(0)=0$ and write the four choices. Preferring A to B says

$$u(1) > 0.10\,u(5)+0.89\,u(1) \iff 0.11\,u(1) > 0.10\,u(5).$$

Preferring D to C says

$$0.10\,u(5) > 0.11\,u(1).$$

The two inequalities are exact negations of each other. No $u$ survives them — not concave, not convex, not any shape you like.

Independence is what manufactures the contradiction: A and B differ from C and D only by replacing a common 89% chance of one million with a common 89% chance of nothing. That shared branch is supposed to cancel. It does not, because the first pair contains a certainty and the second does not.

Prospect theory's reply is to bend the probabilities before they ever multiply a payoff. Episode 2 starts somewhere else entirely — with where you happen to be standing when you choose.

recall.question: Which expected-utility axiom does the Allais pattern violate?

options.text: Independence
options.why: the two pairs differ only by a common branch, which the axiom says must cancel.

options.text: Transitivity
options.why: the choices form two separate pairs, so no preference cycle is ever created.

options.text: Completeness
options.why: subjects have no trouble stating preferences; the trouble is that the two are jointly impossible.

sources.title: Le comportement de l'homme rationnel devant le risque, Econometrica 21(4)
sources.author: Maurice Allais

econ.behavioral.prospect-theory.you-do-n.title: You do not feel wealth. You feel the change.
econ.behavioral.prospect-theory.you-do-n.hook: Your bank balance cannot tell you whether you are happy about your salary. Prospect theory puts that in the arithmetic.
econ.behavioral.prospect-theory.you-do-n.author: author-econ-behavioral-1
econ.behavioral.prospect-theory.you-do-n.body:
Here is something your bank balance cannot tell you: are you happy about your salary? To answer you need what you expected, what you had last year, what the person beside you earns. Prospect theory builds that into the arithmetic. What carries value is not final wealth but the *change* from a reference point.

Two things fall out. First, the same outcome can be a gain or a loss depending on where zero sits — which is why "a 5% raise" and "a 5% raise when everyone else got 10%" are different experiences of the same payslip. Second, the curve through the origin has a kink: losses drop away steeply, gains climb gently. The Cornell mugs are that kink made visible.

Away from zero the curve flattens in both directions. Losing 200 rather than 100 stings less than losing 100 rather than nothing. Steep at the origin, flat in the tails, mirrored — that shape is the whole story, and it has numbers.
econ.behavioral.prospect-theory.you-do-n.rigor:
$$v(x)=\begin{cases} x^{\alpha} & x\ge 0\\[2pt] -\lambda(-x)^{\beta} & x<0\end{cases}$$

where $x$ is measured as a deviation from the reference point. Tversky and Kahneman's 1992 median fit gives $\alpha=\beta=0.88$ and $\lambda=2.25$.

Three properties, each doing work. **Reference dependence**: $v(0)=0$ by construction, so the zero is a modelling choice about the decision-maker's situation, not a fact about the world. **Diminishing sensitivity**: $\alpha,\beta<1$ makes $v$ concave over gains and convex over losses, so an extra unit matters less the further you are from zero — those are the flat tails. **Loss aversion**: $\lambda>1$ tilts the left arm, and at the origin the left derivative is $\lambda$ times the right one. That ratio, about $2.25$, is the kink.

Convexity over losses has a consequence people dislike hearing: it predicts risk *seeking* once you are already behind. Offered a sure loss of 800 or an 85% chance of losing 1000, most people gamble, even though the gamble is worse in expectation. Same curve, other side.

None of this has yet touched the probabilities that multiply $v$. Those turn out to be bent too.

recall.question: In prospect theory, what does the exponent $\alpha<1$ on the gain side produce?

options.text: Diminishing sensitivity
options.why: each extra unit of gain adds less value, so the curve is concave away from the reference point.

options.text: Loss aversion
options.why: that is $\lambda$, the ratio between the slopes on the two sides of zero.

options.text: Probability weighting
options.why: that lives in a separate function applied to probabilities, not to outcomes.

econ.behavioral.replication-crisis.i-pla.title: "I placed too much faith in underpowered studies"
econ.behavioral.replication-crisis.i-pla.hook: In 2017 Kahneman read a blog post taking apart a chapter of his own book, and agreed with it in public.
econ.behavioral.replication-crisis.i-pla.author: author-econ-behavioral-1

reviewed.notes: Quote verified verbatim; the unverifiable 14 February date dropped from the prose and a Retraction Watch source added.

econ.behavioral.replication-crisis.i-pla.body:
*Thinking, Fast and Slow* (2011) presents social priming as settled. In February 2017 Ulrich Schimmack and colleagues published a statistical autopsy of that chapter's sources, titled "Reconstruction of a Train Wreck". Kahneman turned up in the comments days later:

"What the blog gets absolutely right is that I placed too much faith in underpowered studies."

His own first paper with Tversky, in 1971, had warned against trusting samples that are too small. "I failed to internalize its message."

sources.title: Reconstruction of a train wreck: how priming research went off the rails — with Daniel Kahneman's comment of 14 February 2017
sources.author: Schimmack, Heene & Kesavan; comment by Daniel Kahneman

econ.behavioral.replication-crisis.poppe.title: Remember Popper's question? Preregistration is it, in triplicate
econ.behavioral.replication-crisis.poppe.hook: Popper's demarcation asks what would refute you. Preregistration is that question turned into paperwork.
econ.behavioral.replication-crisis.poppe.author: author-econ-behavioral-1
econ.behavioral.replication-crisis.poppe.body:
Remember Popper's demarcation criterion — that a theory earns scientific standing by saying in advance what would refute it? For most of the twentieth century that stayed philosophy. The replication crisis turned it into an administrative form.

The problem it solves is not lying. A perfectly honest researcher with one dataset has dozens of defensible choices: which outliers to drop, which covariates to include, which of four outcome measures to headline, whether to split by gender. Each choice is reasonable on its own. Run them in the order that the data suggest, and you will find a significant result that no amount of integrity makes real. Andrew Gelman calls it the garden of forking paths; there was never a single moment of cheating to point at.

Preregistration closes the garden by making you commit to the path before you see the data. Which is Popper's question, asked at the only time when the answer costs something.
econ.behavioral.replication-crisis.poppe.rigor:
Fix a significance level $\alpha=0.05$. If a researcher runs $m$ independent tests and reports the best one, the probability of at least one false positive under a true null is

$$1-(1-\alpha)^{m},$$

which is $0.23$ at $m=5$ and $0.40$ at $m=10$. Nothing here requires dishonesty: the tests need not be run deliberately, only *selected* after the fact.

The subtler version has no explicit multiplicity at all. If the analysis is chosen as a function of the observed data, the reported $p$-value is no longer the tail probability of the statistic under the null — it is the tail probability of $\max$ over the set of analyses the researcher *would have* run in other datasets. That set is unobservable, which is why the inflation cannot be corrected after the fact.

Preregistration restores the sampling distribution by fixing the analysis before the data exist, making $p$ mean what its definition says. The Popperian content is exact: a preregistration is a written statement of which outcomes would count as refutation, timestamped so that it cannot be rewritten afterwards.

recall.question: Why can a completely honest researcher still produce inflated $p$-values?

options.text: Analysis choices made after seeing the data select the most favourable path
options.why: so the reported $p$ is not the tail probability its definition assumes.

options.text: Because $p$-values are always wrong
options.why: they are exactly right when the analysis is fixed in advance of the data.

options.text: Because small samples bias estimates towards zero
options.why: small samples inflate published estimates, through the significance filter, not shrink them.

econ.behavioral.replication-crisis.what-.title: The scoreboard, and why it is not an argument for cynicism
econ.behavioral.replication-crisis.what-.hook: Psychology replicated 36% of the time. Experimental economics, 61%. The list of survivors is not the list you would guess.
econ.behavioral.replication-crisis.what-.author: author-econ-behavioral-1
econ.behavioral.replication-crisis.what-.body:
Three audits, three numbers. The Open Science Collaboration reran 97 psychology findings in 2015 and got 36% to replicate, with surviving effects about half their original size. Camerer and colleagues reran 18 laboratory economics experiments in 2016: 61%. They then took the social-science papers published in *Nature* and *Science* between 2010 and 2015: around 62%, again at roughly half strength.

Now the specifics, because averages hide the interesting part. Ego depletion — the idea that self-control runs on a depletable fuel — was tested by 23 labs in 2016 and by 36 labs in 2021, and both times the pooled effect was indistinguishable from zero. Several social priming results went the same way. Power posing lost its author's own support.

Loss aversion, anchoring and present bias came through. So did most of the ultimatum-game and public-goods findings. The lesson is not that the field was a fraud. It is that effect sizes published before preregistration were systematically inflated, and the ones built on many independent replications were not.

recall.question: What best explains why published effect sizes shrank on replication?

options.text: Small samples plus selective publication
options.why: an underpowered study only reaches significance with a large estimate, so the record is filtered upward.

options.text: Replication teams were hostile and ran the studies badly
options.why: many replications were preregistered with the original authors' input, and some effects survived intact.

options.text: The effects were all fabricated
options.why: outright fraud is rare; the systematic problem was power and publication filtering.

sources.title: Estimating the reproducibility of psychological science, Science 349(6251)
sources.author: Open Science Collaboration

econ.behavioral.social-preferences.fifte.title: Fifteen societies, one game, and no two played it alike
econ.behavioral.social-preferences.fifte.hook: Mean offers in the ultimatum game ran from 26% to 58% across fifteen small-scale societies. None matched the textbook.
econ.behavioral.social-preferences.fifte.author: author-econ-behavioral-1

reviewed.notes: Added a related link to the Spanish Machiguenga card.

econ.behavioral.social-preferences.fifte.body:
The ultimatum game is two moves long. I propose a split of about a day's wages; you accept and we both get paid, or you refuse and we both get nothing. Self-interest says take anything above zero. Western undergraduates famously do not: they offer 40–45% and reject lowballs out of something that looks a lot like spite.

In the late 1990s a team of anthropologists and economists carried the game to fifteen small-scale societies — Amazonian horticulturalists, Tanzanian foragers, Mongolian herders, Indonesian whale hunters. Group mean offers ran from 26% to 58%. Not one group matched the self-interested prediction, and none of them looked much like the students either.

The Au and Gnau of Papua New Guinea rejected *generous* offers about as readily as stingy ones, in a culture where accepting a large gift creates an obligation you may not want. The Lamalera, who cannot land a whale alone, made the highest offers in the sample.

Two things predicted a group's generosity: how far it was integrated into markets, and how much everyday life rewarded cooperation.

recall.question: What predicted how generously a society played the ultimatum game?

options.text: Market integration and the payoff to cooperation in daily life
options.why: the two group-level variables that tracked mean offers.

options.text: Average household income
options.why: individual-level economic variables did not consistently explain play, within groups or across them.

options.text: Cultural closeness to the West in language or religion
options.why: the pattern tracked economic organisation, not cultural proximity.

sources.title: "Economic man" in cross-cultural perspective: behavioral experiments in 15 small-scale societies, Behavioral and Brain Sciences 28(6)
sources.author: Henrich et al.

econ.behavioral.social-preferences.los-m.title: Los machiguenga aceptaron casi todo, y eso volteó la pregunta
econ.behavioral.social-preferences.los-m.hook: Dieciséis de veintiuna ofertas estuvieron en o por debajo del 30%. Los machiguenga rechazaron cuatro en total.
econ.behavioral.social-preferences.los-m.author: author-econ-behavioral-1

reviewed.notes: Rejection count fixed: Henrich et al. report 16 of 21 offers at or below 30% and four rejections in total, not one. Related link added.

econ.behavioral.social-preferences.los-m.body:
A mediados de los noventa el antropólogo Joseph Henrich llevó el juego del ultimátum a los machiguenga, horticultores de tala y quema de la Amazonía peruana. El juego dura dos movidas: yo propongo un reparto de algo parecido al salario de un día, y usted acepta —cobramos los dos— o rechaza y no cobra nadie.

Entre estudiantes universitarios el resultado es célebre: se ofrece cerca de la mitad y se rechazan las ofertas tacañas por pura indignación. Entre los machiguenga la oferta media fue del 26%, con moda en 15%: dieciséis de veintiuna ofertas estuvieron en o por debajo del 30%, y en total solo se rechazaron cuatro.

El hallazgo obligó a invertir la pregunta. Durante décadas el rechazo indignado se había leído como un universal de la especie. Medido contra quince sociedades de pequeña escala, el caso raro resultamos ser nosotros: gente acostumbrada a cooperar con desconocidos, a comprar en mercados anónimos y a castigar sin costo a quien se pasa de vivo. Los machiguenga viven en familias casi autosuficientes, donde nada de eso hace falta.

recall.question: ¿Qué invirtió el resultado machiguenga en la lectura del juego del ultimátum?
recall.answer: Que rechazar una oferta injusta no es un universal humano sino una conducta ligada a sociedades con mucho mercado y mucha cooperación entre desconocidos. Frente a las quince sociedades estudiadas, el caso atípico es el estudiante occidental.

econ.behavioral.social-preferences.stran.title: Remember Hamilton's rule? Strangers share none of your genes
econ.behavioral.social-preferences.stran.hook: Hamilton's rule explains why you would die for two brothers. It predicts zero for an anonymous stranger. People give anyway.
econ.behavioral.social-preferences.stran.author: author-econ-behavioral-1

reviewed.notes: Added Fehr and Schmidt (1999) as the source for the inequity-aversion function used in the rigor layer.

econ.behavioral.social-preferences.stran.body:
Remember Hamilton's rule — altruism pays when $rB>C$, with $r$ the fraction of your genome the beneficiary carries? It handles a worker bee and a ground squirrel's alarm call beautifully. Now point it at somebody handing money to an anonymous stranger, in a one-shot laboratory game, with nobody watching and no chance of meeting again.

Here $r\approx 0$, the benefit lands on someone else, and the cost is real. Hamilton's rule says: give nothing. Across fifteen societies the mean offer was never nothing.

The explanations are genuinely in dispute. One camp says the machinery is misfiring — our instincts were shaped in small groups where nobody was ever truly anonymous or truly one-shot, so the laboratory is an evolutionary optical illusion. Another says the preference is real, built by culture and competition between groups, and that people simply value fairness.

Either way economics needs a utility function that does not maximise own money. The standard one has a shape worth knowing.
econ.behavioral.social-preferences.stran.rigor:
Hamilton's rule is a condition on inclusive fitness: a helping allele spreads when $rB>C$, with $r$ the relatedness coefficient, $B$ the recipient's fitness gain and $C$ the actor's cost. For anonymous strangers $r\to 0$ and the inequality fails for every $C>0$.

Economists instead fit **inequity aversion**. Fehr and Schmidt's two-player form is

$$U_i(x)=x_i-\alpha_i\max\{x_j-x_i,\,0\}-\beta_i\max\{x_i-x_j,\,0\},\qquad \beta_i\le\alpha_i,\ \ 0\le\beta_i<1,$$

where $\alpha_i$ measures how much you dislike having less than the other player and $\beta_i$ how much you dislike having more.

One function reproduces both halves of the ultimatum game. A responder offered 20 out of 100 compares $20-\alpha_i(80-20)$ with $0$, so anyone with $\alpha_i>1/3$ refuses. A proposer who anticipates that offers just enough to clear the threshold. And a proposer with $\beta_i>1/2$ hands over half even when refusal is impossible, which is what dictator games show.

Notice what the model does not do: it puts fairness in the preferences and says nothing about where the preferences came from. For kin, Hamilton's rule answers that. For strangers, the argument is open.

recall.question: Why is Hamilton's rule not an explanation of giving in one-shot anonymous games?

options.text: Relatedness is essentially zero
options.why: so $rB>C$ fails for any positive cost and the rule predicts nothing is given.

options.text: Hamilton's rule applies only to insects
options.why: it is a general condition on inclusive fitness, derived for any population.

options.text: Laboratory stakes are too small to matter
options.why: the same pattern shows up when the stake is a day's or a week's wages.

sources.title: A theory of fairness, competition, and cooperation, Quarterly Journal of Economics 114(3)
sources.author: Fehr & Schmidt

econ.behavioral.time-discounting.save-mo.title: The savings plan that only asks for money you do not have yet
econ.behavioral.time-discounting.save-mo.hook: The plan asks for none of the money you have. It asks for a slice of the raise you have not received yet.
econ.behavioral.time-discounting.save-mo.author: author-econ-behavioral-1
econ.behavioral.time-discounting.save-mo.body:
Saving more hurts now and pays later, which is the one shape human beings handle worst. Richard Thaler and Shlomo Benartzi's answer was to stop fighting that and design around it.

Their SMarT plan — Save More Tomorrow — asks employees to commit today to raising their retirement contribution *at their next pay rise*, and at every rise after that. Three biases switch sides. Present bias: the cost sits in the future, where it barely registers. Loss aversion: contributions climb only when take-home pay climbs, so nobody ever watches a paycheque shrink. Inertia: the escalation continues by default, and stopping it requires an action nobody gets around to.

At the first company that ran it, employees who joined went from saving 3.5% of pay to 13.6% by their fourth raise. Published in the *Journal of Political Economy* in 2004, it became one of the most copied ideas in retirement policy — and the cleanest case of a nudge that recruits a bias instead of lecturing it.

recall.question: Which three behavioural forces does Save More Tomorrow recruit rather than fight?
recall.answer: Present bias — the cost is deferred. Loss aversion — the contribution rises only out of a raise, so take-home pay never falls. Inertia — the escalation runs by default until you opt out.

sources.title: Save More Tomorrow: using behavioral economics to increase employee saving, Journal of Political Economy 112(S1)
sources.author: Thaler & Benartzi

econ.behavioral.time-discounting.the-pig.title: The choice you make for next year is not the one you will make
econ.behavioral.time-discounting.the-pig.hook: Same six-month wait, moved three months into the future, and the answer flips. Pigeons do it too.
econ.behavioral.time-discounting.the-pig.author: author-econ-behavioral-1
econ.behavioral.time-discounting.the-pig.body:
Would you rather have 50 today or 100 in six months? Plenty of people take the 50. Now: 50 in three months, or 100 in nine months? Same six-month wait, pushed three months into the future — and most of the people who took the 50 now take the 100.

Nothing about the trade-off changed except its distance from you. That is a preference reversal, and it is fatal to exponential discounting, where a constant per-period rate makes the two questions literally the same question. Pigeons reverse too, which was Ainslie's point in the 1970s: this is the shape of the discount curve, not a quirk of human culture.

Thaler's 1981 study put numbers on the slope. Subjects indifferent between \$15 now, \$30 in three months, \$60 in a year and \$100 in three years are implying annual discount rates of 277%, then 139%, then 63%. Your future self is patient. Your present self is not, and it is the one holding the pen.

One extra parameter is enough to model it.
econ.behavioral.time-discounting.the-pig.rigor:
Exponential discounting values a payoff $x$ at delay $t$ as $\delta^{t}x$. The ratio between two delayed payoffs then depends only on the gap between the dates: $\delta^{t_2}/\delta^{t_1}=\delta^{t_2-t_1}$. Shift both dates by the same amount and nothing moves, so reversal is impossible. That is exactly the property the data kill.

Laibson's 1997 quasi-hyperbolic form keeps the algebra and adds one number:

$$D(t)=\begin{cases}1 & t=0\\ \beta\delta^{t} & t\ge 1\end{cases}\qquad 0<\beta\le 1.$$

Everything that is not now takes an extra flat haircut $\beta$. Comparing today with tomorrow you face $\beta\delta$; comparing day $t$ with day $t+1$ from a distance you face $\delta$. One rate at the now/not-now boundary, another everywhere else.

The reversal drops out. Taking 50 today over 100 in six months means $50>100\beta\delta^{6}$; taking 100 in nine months over 50 in three means $100\delta^{6}>50$. Both hold at once exactly when

$$100\beta\delta^{6}<50<100\delta^{6},$$

which has solutions if and only if $\beta<1$. The patient future self is $\delta$. The impatient present self is $\beta$.

recall.question: Why can exponential discounting never produce a preference reversal?

options.text: Its discount ratio depends only on the gap between dates
options.why: shifting both dates equally leaves every comparison unchanged.

options.text: It assumes people are patient
options.why: it allows any level of impatience; what it forbids is impatience that changes with distance.

options.text: It ignores the size of the payoffs
options.why: payoffs enter normally; the constraint is on how time enters.

sources.title: Golden eggs and hyperbolic discounting, Quarterly Journal of Economics 112(2)
sources.author: David Laibson

econ.causal.credibility-revolution.nobod.title: "Hardly anyone takes anyone else's data analyses seriously"
econ.causal.credibility-revolution.nobod.hook: The most quoted sentence ever written about applied economics was an insult, and the profession agreed with it.
econ.causal.credibility-revolution.nobod.author: author-econ-metrics-1

reviewed.notes: The quote is on p. 37, not the opening, and reads data analyses. Restored verbatim from the AER text and extended with the plumed-birds line.

econ.causal.credibility-revolution.nobod.body:
Edward Leamer, halfway through his 1983 *American Economic Review* broadside: "Hardly anyone takes data analyses seriously. Or perhaps more accurately, hardly anyone takes anyone else's data analyses seriously. Like elaborately plumed birds who have long since lost the ability to procreate but not the desire, we preen and strut and display our t-values."

His target: specification search — fitting the regression many ways, reporting the one that behaved. Twenty-seven years later Angrist and Pischke borrowed his title to announce the fix: argue about where the variation came from.

econ.causal.credibility-revolution.takin.title: The decade economics stopped believing its own regressions
econ.causal.credibility-revolution.takin.hook: In 1983 an economist told his colleagues that nobody believed anybody's regressions. He was right, and it worked.
econ.causal.credibility-revolution.takin.author: author-econ-metrics-1

reviewed.notes: Leamer wording fixed (analyses). Deaton and Heckman wrote in a JEL symposium, not the same issue as Angrist-Pischke, which was JEP.

econ.causal.credibility-revolution.takin.body:
Edward Leamer's 1983 complaint was that econometrics had become a search: try controls until the coefficient behaves, report the run that survived, call it evidence. Hardly anyone, he wrote, takes anyone else's data analyses seriously — and everybody knew he was describing the whole profession.

The answer was not better statistics. It was to stop asking "what should I control for?" and start asking "where did the variation come from?" A state line. A lottery. A rule with a cutoff. A pipe laid in 1852. Angrist and Pischke called it the credibility revolution in 2010, and in 2021 the Nobel committee agreed, honouring Card, Angrist and Imbens for exactly this.

The critics are worth as much as the converts. Angus Deaton and James Heckman argued the same year, in the *Journal of Economic Literature*, that a clean local effect on a lucky subgroup can be less useful than a messier estimate of the thing you actually want to know. Both objections are live.

Snow never asked what to control for. He asked who laid the pipes.
econ.causal.credibility-revolution.takin.rigor:
The design-based programme is one sentence about identification: pick an estimand, then find a source of variation $Z$ for which "as good as random" is defendable, and accept the estimand $Z$ gives you. Formally you trade assumptions of the form "$Y(0)$ is mean-independent of $D$ given my controls $X$" — untestable and usually false — for assumptions about a known mechanism.

What you pay is in the estimand. An instrument or a discontinuity identifies an effect for **compliers** or for units *at* the cutoff, not for everyone: $\mathbb{E}[Y(1)-Y(0)\mid \text{complier}]$ is not $\mathbb{E}[Y(1)-Y(0)]$. Scaling that up needs either a model of how effects vary with covariates, or the assumption that they do not — which is where Deaton's and Heckman's objection lands, and where structural modelling re-enters.

The rest of this domain is the toolkit: instruments, discontinuities, panels, synthetic controls. Each one is an argument about the selection-bias term in episode 3.

recall.question: What changed in empirical economics after Leamer's critique?

options.text: Researchers began justifying their estimates by the source of variation
options.why: lotteries, cutoffs, borders — rather than by the list of controls in the regression. — design first, estimation second.

options.text: Economists switched to larger datasets, which removed the bias.
options.why: bias does not shrink with sample size; that was the point.

options.text: Regression was abandoned in favour of machine learning.
options.why: regression is still the workhorse; what changed is what justifies it.

options.text: Researchers started reporting p-values more carefully.
options.why: better inference on a badly identified estimate is still a badly identified estimate.
