econ.game-theory.mechanism-design.just-a.title: Any mechanism can be replaced by one where lying is pointless
econ.game-theory.mechanism-design.just-a.hook: Whatever your clever multi-stage procedure achieves, a form that people fill in honestly achieves the same thing.
econ.game-theory.mechanism-design.just-a.author: author-econ-behavioral-1
econ.game-theory.mechanism-design.just-a.body:
You are designing a rule — an auction, a voting system, a way to allocate kidneys — and you are worried about the obvious thing: people will misrepresent what they want in order to game it. So you start sketching elaborate multi-stage procedures to smoke out the truth.

Stop. The revelation principle says that whatever outcome your elaborate procedure produces in equilibrium, there is a *direct* mechanism — everyone reports their private information once, the designer computes the outcome — that produces exactly the same outcome, and in which reporting honestly is an equilibrium.

The argument is almost insultingly simple. Whatever strategy each type would have played inside your clever mechanism, build that strategy into the rule. The mechanism now does the lying on everyone's behalf, so nobody has to.

It is the most useful theorem in mechanism design, and its usefulness points backwards: if no honest mechanism can reach your goal, no dishonest one can either.
econ.game-theory.mechanism-design.just-a.rigor:
Fix types $\theta_i\in\Theta_i$ drawn from a common prior, and a **mechanism** $\Gamma=(M_1,\dots,M_n,g)$ with message spaces $M_i$ and outcome function $g:\prod_i M_i\to X$. Suppose $\Gamma$ has a Bayesian Nash equilibrium $m^{*}$, with $m^{*}_i:\Theta_i\to M_i$, implementing the social choice function $f(\theta)=g(m^{*}(\theta))$.

**Revelation principle.** The direct mechanism with $M_i=\Theta_i$ and outcome function $f$ has truth-telling as a Bayesian Nash equilibrium, and implements the same $f$.

*Proof.* Suppose type $\theta_i$ gained by reporting $\hat\theta_i$ in the direct mechanism. Then in $\Gamma$, type $\theta_i$ would have gained by sending $m^{*}_i(\hat\theta_i)$ rather than $m^{*}_i(\theta_i)$, since the two induce identical outcome distributions against $m^{*}_{-i}$. That contradicts $m^{*}$ being an equilibrium. $\square$

The power lies in what it rules out. To show that *no* mechanism achieves some goal, it now suffices to check the incentive-compatible direct ones — a finite system of inequalities instead of a search over all conceivable institutions. That is how the impossibility theorems get proved: Gibbard–Satterthwaite for voting, Myerson–Satterthwaite for efficient bilateral trade.

Two cautions. It is a statement about equilibria, so a mechanism with several of them is replicated only at the one you selected. And truth-telling becomes *an* equilibrium, not the unique or a dominant one, unless you demand more.

recall.question: Why is the revelation principle used mostly to prove impossibility results?

options.text: It shrinks the search from all mechanisms to incentive-compatible direct ones
options.why: so ruling those out rules out everything.

options.text: It shows an honest mechanism exists for any goal
options.why: it says nothing about whether the goal is reachable at all.

options.text: It makes truth-telling a dominant strategy
options.why: it makes truth-telling an equilibrium, which is strictly weaker.

sources.title: Incentive compatibility and the bargaining problem, Econometrica 47(1)
sources.author: Roger Myerson

econ.game-theory.mixed-strategies.matchi.title: The game with no answer until you agree to be unpredictable
econ.game-theory.mixed-strategies.matchi.hook: Your equilibrium mixture is not determined by your payoffs. It is determined by your opponent's.
econ.game-theory.mixed-strategies.matchi.author: author-econ-behavioral-1
econ.game-theory.mixed-strategies.matchi.body:
Two players each slap down a coin. Faces match, I take both; faces differ, you do. Try to find a stable pair of choices. Heads–heads? You should have played tails. Heads–tails? I should have played tails. Walk round the four cells and you never stop moving.

Matching pennies has no equilibrium in the ordinary sense, and that failure is not a technicality. It is the defining feature of every game where one player wants to be guessed wrong. A goalkeeper with a favourite side is a goalkeeper who has been scouted.

Nash's repair is to widen what counts as a strategy: choose probabilities, not actions. Now an equilibrium exists — both randomise fifty-fifty, and neither can do better.

The strange part is *why* fifty-fifty is right. Not because it maximises your payoff. Because it makes your opponent indifferent.
econ.game-theory.mixed-strategies.matchi.rigor:
In a mixed equilibrium every action a player uses with positive probability must earn exactly the same expected payoff; otherwise shifting weight onto the best of them would be an improvement. That is the **indifference principle**, and it is what you actually solve.

Matching pennies: I win 1 when the coins match, my opponent wins 1 when they differ. Let $q$ be the probability my opponent plays heads. My expected payoff from heads is $q-(1-q)=2q-1$; from tails it is $(1-q)-q=1-2q$. For me to be willing to mix at all these must be equal, so $q=1/2$. Symmetrically, my own probability $p$ must equal $1/2$ to keep my opponent willing to mix.

Read what just happened. My probability is pinned down by *my opponent's* indifference condition, not by my own payoffs. Double my prize for matching heads and my equilibrium mixture does not move; my opponent's does. In equilibrium your randomisation exists to kill their incentive to deviate, not to serve you.

The value of the game to me is $0$, and von Neumann's minimax theorem (1928) says every finite two-player zero-sum game has such a value, attained in mixed strategies. Nash generalised it past zero-sum.

Existence was the win. The bill arrives in episode 3: allow sequencing and games acquire *too many* equilibria, some of them plainly absurd.

recall.question: In a mixed-strategy equilibrium, what pins down your probabilities?

options.text: Your opponent's indifference condition
options.why: you mix in exactly the way that leaves them with no reason to switch.

options.text: Your own payoffs
options.why: change your prizes and your equilibrium mixture stays put; theirs is what moves.

options.text: Nothing in particular, since any mixture works
options.why: only the indifference-inducing mixture is stable against deviation.

econ.game-theory.mixed-strategies.profes.title: Penalty kicks are the best experiment game theory ever got
econ.game-theory.mixed-strategies.profes.hook: More than 1,400 professional penalties, and both halves of von Neumann's minimax theorem survived the test.
econ.game-theory.mixed-strategies.profes.author: author-econ-behavioral-1
econ.game-theory.mixed-strategies.profes.body:
A penalty is a two-person zero-sum game with simultaneous moves, played by professionals who have rehearsed it thousands of times, for stakes that end careers. Game theory has rarely had a laboratory that good.

Ignacio Palacios-Huerta gathered more than 1,400 penalties from professional leagues and tested the two things minimax actually predicts. First, scoring probabilities should be equal across the strategies a player genuinely uses: if kicking left scored more often than kicking right, kickers would go left more until goalkeepers adjusted and the rates levelled. Second, choices should be serially independent — no alternating, no streaks, nothing a scout could sell.

Both held. Winning probabilities were statistically identical across strategies, and serial independence could not be rejected, in tests with real power against the obvious alternatives.

It is the first time both implications of the minimax theorem passed in a natural setting. None of the players could state the theorem. They had simply been punished for years for being predictable.
econ.game-theory.mixed-strategies.profes.rigor:
A two-player zero-sum game with payoff matrix $A$ has a **value**

$$v=\max_{p\in\Delta(S_1)}\ \min_{q\in\Delta(S_2)}\ p^{\top}Aq\;=\;\min_{q}\ \max_{p}\ p^{\top}Aq,$$

by von Neumann's minimax theorem (1928). Two testable consequences follow for the equilibrium mixtures.

**Equal payoffs across used strategies.** If $p^{*}_i>0$ then $(Aq^{*})_i=v$. A kicker who truly mixes between left and right must therefore score at the same rate with each. Note that this is a restriction on *outcomes*, not on frequencies: it holds even though optimal mixtures are nowhere near fifty-fifty, because kickers have a stronger side and everyone knows it.

**Serial independence.** The equilibrium is one fixed mixture played i.i.d. across repetitions. Any dependence on the previous kick — alternating, streaking, reacting to the last save — is exploitable, so equilibrium forbids it.

The second test is the brutal one, because people asked to generate random sequences alternate far too much. These professionals did not. Keep the boundary of the result in view: it says experienced players in a well-practised, high-stakes, strictly competitive game land on the equilibrium. It says nothing about anyone meeting a new game for the first time, where the evidence runs firmly the other way.

recall.question: Why does minimax predict equal scoring rates across a kicker's strategies?

options.text: Any strategy used with positive probability must earn the value of the game
options.why: otherwise the kicker would shift weight onto the better one.

options.text: Because the kicker mixes fifty-fifty
options.why: optimal mixtures here are not fifty-fifty; the prediction is about rates, not frequencies.

options.text: Because goalkeepers dive at random
options.why: goalkeepers play their own optimal and generally unequal mixture.

sources.title: Professionals play minimax, Review of Economic Studies 70(2)
sources.author: Ignacio Palacios-Huerta

econ.game-theory.repeated-games.live-and.title: The trenches invented cooperation without meaning to
econ.game-theory.repeated-games.live-and.hook: Two armies trying to kill each other stopped, without a word being exchanged, because they expected to meet again tomorrow.
econ.game-theory.repeated-games.live-and.author: author-econ-behavioral-1
econ.game-theory.repeated-games.live-and.body:
By 1915 stretches of the Western Front had settled into something high command detested. British and German units facing each other across a few hundred metres had quietly stopped trying to kill one another. Rations came up at predictable hours and nobody shelled them. Artillery hit the same patch of ground at the same time each day, so everyone knew where to stand. Snipers missed on purpose.

The historian Tony Ashworth documented the system; Robert Axelrod used it in 1984 as the best real-world case of cooperation emerging between enemies with no communication, no trust, and every order to shoot.

The mechanism is repetition. The same two units faced each other for months, so restraint today bought restraint tomorrow. Headquarters broke it the only way it could: rotating units and ordering raids that forced casualties, destroying the single ingredient cooperation needed.

recall.question: Which ingredient did headquarters destroy, and why did that work?
recall.answer: The shadow of the future. Cooperation in a repeated game depends on expecting to meet the same opponent again; a unit that will be moved next week, and is ordered to inflict casualties this week, has no future relationship left to protect.

sources.title: Live and let live (World War I)

econ.game-theory.repeated-games.the-folk.title: Everything is an equilibrium, if the game never ends
econ.game-theory.repeated-games.the-folk.hook: Repetition explains cooperation. It also explains almost every other pattern of behaviour, which is the problem.
econ.game-theory.repeated-games.the-folk.author: author-econ-behavioral-1
econ.game-theory.repeated-games.the-folk.body:
In a one-shot prisoner's dilemma, defection is the only equilibrium and cooperation is wishful thinking. Play the same game every day forever and cooperation becomes an equilibrium: I cooperate because I expect you to, and because I know what happens to me if I stop.

Good. The trouble is what *else* becomes an equilibrium. I cooperate on Mondays and defect on Thursdays — equilibrium. You take 90% of the surplus and I take 10% — equilibrium. Almost any pattern you can describe, provided it pays each of us at least what we could guarantee alone, is supportable by some arrangement of threats.

That is the folk theorem, so named because it circulated among game theorists for years before anybody troubled to publish it. It is at once the field's most celebrated result and its most awkward: repetition explains cooperation, and repetition explains nearly everything else, which is uncomfortably close to explaining nothing.

The content is in the precise statement.
econ.game-theory.repeated-games.the-folk.rigor:
Fix a finite stage game with payoffs $u_i$. Player $i$'s **minmax** value is

$$\underline{v}_i=\min_{\sigma_{-i}}\ \max_{a_i}\ u_i(a_i,\sigma_{-i}),$$

the most $i$ can guarantee when everyone else is trying to hold them down. A payoff vector $v$ is *individually rational* if $v_i>\underline{v}_i$ for every $i$, and *feasible* if it is a convex combination of stage-game payoff vectors. Let $V^{*}$ be the set of feasible, strictly individually rational payoffs.

**Folk theorem (Fudenberg and Maskin, 1986).** If $V^{*}$ has full dimension $|N|$, then for every $v\in V^{*}$ there is $\underline{\delta}<1$ such that for all discount factors $\delta\in(\underline{\delta},1)$, $v$ is the average payoff of some subgame-perfect equilibrium of the infinitely repeated game.

Two conditions carry the weight. *Patience*: with $\delta$ near 1 the one-period gain from cheating is negligible against a permanent loss. *Full dimensionality*: it lets a punishment hurt one player while still rewarding the punishers, so that carrying out the punishment is itself credible — without it the threat has exactly the price-war problem.

Grim trigger in a prisoner's dilemma with payoffs $3$ for mutual cooperation, $1$ for mutual defection, $4$ for cheating and $0$ for being cheated: cooperation holds when $3/(1-\delta)\ge 4+\delta/(1-\delta)$, that is $\delta\ge 1/3$.

recall.question: What is the full-dimensionality condition doing in the folk theorem?

options.text: It lets a punishment hurt one player while rewarding the punishers
options.why: so carrying out the threat is itself credible.

options.text: It makes the equilibrium payoff unique
options.why: the theorem delivers the opposite: a continuum of supportable payoffs.

options.text: It allows players to randomise
options.why: mixing is available whatever the dimension of the payoff set.

sources.title: The folk theorem in repeated games with discounting or with incomplete information, Econometrica 54(3)
sources.author: Fudenberg & Maskin

econ.game-theory.signaling.the-degree-th.title: A degree worth paying for even if it teaches you nothing
econ.game-theory.signaling.the-degree-th.hook: Spence's model assumes education adds nothing to productivity — and concludes that buying it is still rational.
econ.game-theory.signaling.the-degree-th.author: author-econ-behavioral-1
econ.game-theory.signaling.the-degree-th.body:
Suppose university taught you nothing whatsoever. Would going still be rational? Michael Spence's 1973 answer is yes, and it leans on no hidden benefit at all.

Employers cannot see how productive you are. You can. If a degree is *cheaper* for productive people than for unproductive ones — less effort, fewer repeats, less misery — then it can carry information while carrying no skill. High types buy it; low types decide the price is not worth the wage it unlocks; employers read the certificate and pay accordingly; and the beliefs that made them pay turn out to be correct.

That is a separating equilibrium, and the unsettling part is how stable it is. Nobody is deceived. Everybody behaves optimally. And a great deal of money has been spent to transmit roughly one bit of information.

Spence shared the 2001 Nobel for it. What makes it work is a single inequality about costs.
econ.game-theory.signaling.the-degree-th.rigor:
Two worker types $\theta\in\{\theta_L,\theta_H\}$ with $\theta_H>\theta_L$. Education $e\ge 0$ costs the worker $c(e,\theta)$ and adds nothing to output, so a worker of type $\theta$ produces $\theta$ whatever they study. Competitive employers pay expected productivity given the observed signal.

The **single-crossing** condition is

$$\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\!\left(\frac{\partial c}{\partial e}\right)<0,$$

the marginal cost of education falls as type rises. The textbook choice $c(e,\theta)=e/\theta$ satisfies it.

A separating equilibrium is a threshold $e^{*}$: employers pay $\theta_H$ when $e\ge e^{*}$ and $\theta_L$ otherwise. It survives when neither type wants to switch,

$$\theta_H-\frac{e^{*}}{\theta_H}\ \ge\ \theta_L \qquad\text{and}\qquad \theta_L\ \ge\ \theta_H-\frac{e^{*}}{\theta_L},$$

which forces $e^{*}\in\bigl[\theta_L(\theta_H-\theta_L),\ \theta_H(\theta_H-\theta_L)\bigr]$ — a continuum of equilibria, one per admissible threshold.

Two things to carry away. The outcome is inefficient: total output is unchanged and $e^{*}>0$ is pure deadweight spent on sorting. And the multiplicity is not a modelling defect but a fact about signals: beliefs are self-confirming, so every threshold in that interval is held up by beliefs that make it true.

recall.question: What must hold for education to work as a signal even when it teaches nothing?

options.text: It is cheaper for high-productivity workers
options.why: single crossing is what stops low types buying the same certificate.

options.text: It is expensive for everybody
options.why: a uniformly high cost separates nobody; the cost has to differ by type.

options.text: Employers cannot observe education
options.why: they must observe it. What they cannot observe is productivity.

sources.title: Job market signaling, Quarterly Journal of Economics 87(3)
sources.author: Michael Spence

econ.game-theory.social-choice.what-arro.title: Remember Arrow's theorem? Here is what it actually forbids
econ.game-theory.social-choice.what-arro.hook: "There is no perfect voting system" is not what Arrow proved, and the difference is where all the interesting work is.
econ.game-theory.social-choice.what-arro.author: author-econ-behavioral-1
econ.game-theory.social-choice.what-arro.body:
Remember Arrow's impossibility theorem — the one everyone summarises as "there is no perfect voting system"? That summary does real damage, because the theorem is far more specific, and far more interesting, than the slogan.

Arrow is not about a single election. It is about a *rule* that takes everybody's full ranking of all the candidates and returns one social ranking, for every conceivable profile of individual rankings. With three or more alternatives, four mild-sounding requirements on such a rule are jointly impossible, and the proof does something stronger than say "impossible": it locates a dictator.

What the theorem does not say: that majority rule is bad, that voting is pointless, or that all systems are equally flawed. Approval and range voting escape by using more than rankings. Single-peaked preferences escape by shrinking the domain. Every escape from Arrow is an escape from one specific hypothesis, which is why the hypotheses repay careful reading.

The one everybody fights about is the third.
econ.game-theory.social-choice.what-arro.rigor:
Let $A$ be a set of alternatives with $|A|\ge 3$ and $N$ a finite set of voters. A **social welfare function** $F$ maps each profile $(\succ_1,\dots,\succ_n)$ of complete transitive individual rankings to a complete transitive social ranking.

**Theorem (Arrow, 1950, 1951).** No $F$ satisfies all four of:

1. **Unrestricted domain** — $F$ is defined on every profile of complete transitive rankings.
2. **Weak Pareto** — if every voter ranks $a$ above $b$, society does too.
3. **Independence of irrelevant alternatives** — society's ranking of $a$ against $b$ depends only on how voters rank $a$ against $b$.
4. **Non-dictatorship** — no single voter's strict ranking always becomes society's.

Condition 3 is the contested one. It is what kills the Borda count and anything using intensity: if a voter shifts $c$ about without touching $a$ versus $b$, the social verdict on $a$ versus $b$ must not move.

The standard proof builds a **decisive set**. Show some coalition is decisive over some pair; use unrestricted domain and IIA to spread decisiveness from one pair to all pairs; then shrink the decisive set one voter at a time until a single voter remains. That voter is the dictator.

Gibbard and Satterthwaite later proved the strategic twin: any voting rule with at least three possible winners that is not dictatorial can be manipulated by a voter who misreports. Arrow constrains aggregation, Gibbard–Satterthwaite constrains honesty, and they are the same obstruction seen from two sides.

recall.question: Which Arrow condition rules out the Borda count?

options.text: Independence of irrelevant alternatives
options.why: Borda scores depend on where the other candidates sit, so moving a third one can flip $a$ against $b$.

options.text: Weak Pareto
options.why: Borda respects unanimity perfectly well.

options.text: Unrestricted domain
options.why: Borda is defined on every profile of rankings, so that is not where it fails.

econ.game-theory.subgame-perfection.thre.title: The equilibrium where you threaten what you would never do
econ.game-theory.subgame-perfection.thre.hook: "Enter my market and I will destroy us both" is a Nash equilibrium. That is a problem with Nash equilibrium.
econ.game-theory.subgame-perfection.thre.author: author-econ-behavioral-1
econ.game-theory.subgame-perfection.thre.body:
A new firm is thinking about entering your market. You announce that if they come in, you will cut prices until neither of you makes a peso. They stay out. Now check the definition: nobody can do better by changing their own strategy alone. This is a Nash equilibrium.

It is also nonsense. If they *did* enter, a price war would gut you too, and everyone in the room knows it. Your threat is not a plan. It is a sentence.

Nash equilibrium cannot see the difference, because it only asks whether a deviation would pay *given* what everyone has said they will do. It never checks whether the announcement would survive contact with an actual entrant. Reinhard Selten's fix, in 1965, was to insist that a profile be an equilibrium not only of the whole game but of every subgame — including the ones that equilibrium play never reaches.

That single requirement deletes the threat. It also deletes rather more than anyone expected.
econ.game-theory.subgame-perfection.thre.rigor:
Let $G$ be a finite extensive-form game. A **subgame** is a subtree rooted at a single node such that every information set of $G$ lies entirely inside it or entirely outside it. A profile is **subgame perfect** if its restriction to every subgame is a Nash equilibrium of that subgame.

The entry game. The entrant chooses In or Out; if In, the incumbent chooses Fight or Accommodate. Payoffs: Out gives $(0,2)$, (In, Accommodate) gives $(1,1)$, (In, Fight) gives $(-1,-1)$.

There are two Nash equilibria. In $(\text{Out},\text{Fight})$ the entrant prefers $0$ to $-1$ given Fight, and the incumbent's plan is never tested, so no deviation pays. The other is $(\text{In},\text{Accommodate})$.

Only the second survives. The subgame after In is a one-player choice between $1$ and $-1$, and Fight is not a Nash equilibrium of it. In games of perfect information, subgame perfection is exactly backward induction.

Two things to keep. It is a *refinement*: it never creates equilibria, only removes them, so existence comes free from Nash. And it is demanding in precisely the way the centipede exposed, since it insists on optimal play in subgames nobody ever visits.

Episode 4 removes the last comfortable assumption — that everyone knows which game they are in.

recall.question: Why is "enter and I will fight" not subgame perfect?

options.text: In the subgame after entry, fighting is not optimal
options.why: so the plan is not a Nash equilibrium of that subgame, though it is one of the whole game.

options.text: Because it is not a Nash equilibrium
options.why: it is one, which is exactly the problem subgame perfection was invented to fix.

options.text: Because the entrant cannot observe the threat
options.why: the threat is announced and understood; what it lacks is credibility, not publicity.

econ.game-theory.what-is-a-game.born-in-.title: The prisoner's dilemma was invented to embarrass Nash
econ.game-theory.what-is-a-game.born-in-.hook: The most famous game in social science was invented to show that Nash equilibrium does not predict what people do.
econ.game-theory.what-is-a-game.born-in-.author: author-econ-behavioral-1
econ.game-theory.what-is-a-game.born-in-.body:
In 1950 two mathematicians at the RAND Corporation in Santa Monica, Merrill Flood and Melvin Dresher, wrote down a small two-player game. They were not looking for a parable about trust. They were testing whether the equilibrium concept John Nash had just published described what people would actually do.

They ran it a hundred times with two colleagues — the economist Armen Alchian and the mathematician John Williams — and kept the players' running commentary. The players cooperated far more often than the equilibrium allowed, and complained bitterly at each other when they did not. RAND worked on nuclear strategy; nobody there thought this was an academic curiosity.

It was Albert Tucker who gave the matrix the story that made it famous: two prisoners, separate cells, a prosecutor offering each one a deal. Not a single payoff changed. The name did, and that is why you have heard of it.

recall.question: What did Flood and Dresher's hundred rounds actually show?
recall.answer: That two well-informed players cooperate far more often than the equilibrium predicts, and resent each other when they do not. The game was built as a test of Nash equilibrium as a description of behaviour, and it failed that test on day one.

econ.game-theory.what-is-a-game.real-lif.title: "Chess is not a game"
econ.game-theory.what-is-a-game.real-lif.hook: Von Neumann did not think chess was a game. He thought poker was.
econ.game-theory.what-is-a-game.real-lif.author: author-econ-behavioral-1
econ.game-theory.what-is-a-game.real-lif.body:
Jacob Bronowski shared a wartime taxi with John von Neumann and asked about his theory of games. *The Ascent of Man* (1973) reports the answer:

"Chess is not a game. Chess is a well-defined form of computation… Real life consists of bluffing, of little tactics of deception, of asking yourself what is the other man going to think I mean to do."

Bronowski was recalling, not transcribing. But the distinction splits the field: perfect information is an algorithm problem; private information is game theory.

sources.title: John von Neumann quotations — sourced to Jacob Bronowski, The Ascent of Man (1973), 324
sources.author: Jacob Bronowski

econ.game-theory.what-is-a-game.the-doll.title: I am auctioning a dollar, and the runner-up pays too
econ.game-theory.what-is-a-game.the-doll.hook: I am auctioning a one-dollar bill. The winner pays their bid. So does the runner-up.
econ.game-theory.what-is-a-game.the-doll.author: author-econ-behavioral-1
econ.game-theory.what-is-a-game.the-doll.body:
The rules. I auction a one-dollar bill in five-cent steps. Highest bidder wins the dollar and pays their bid. Here is the twist: the *second*-highest bidder also pays their bid, and gets nothing at all.

Bidding five cents for a dollar is obviously worth it. So is ten. Now suppose the bidding has reached 90 cents and someone bids 95. You are about to lose 90 cents for nothing — and bidding one dollar turns that into breaking even. So you bid a dollar. Now *they* are about to lose 95 cents for nothing, and bidding 1.05 turns a 95-cent loss into a 5-cent loss.

Martin Shubik published this in 1971 and ran it on students for years. Where does it stop — and what exactly was the mistake?

recall.question: Where does the bidding stop, and which bid was the error?
recall.answer: It does not stop on its own: from any position, one more bid beats conceding, so the escalation stays locally rational far past a dollar. The error is the *first* bid, which commits you to a contest where the loser pays. Shubik's target was escalation in general — sunk costs plus a penalty for coming second is the structure of price wars, patent races and wars.

sources.title: The dollar auction game: a paradox in noncooperative behavior and escalation, Journal of Conflict Resolution 15(1)
sources.author: Martin Shubik

econ.history-thought.colombian-economy.e.title: El profesor que rediseñó el Estado colombiano en unos meses
econ.history-thought.colombian-economy.e.hook: En 1923 Colombia no tenía banco central. Un profesor de Princeton llegó en marzo y se fue habiendo creado tres instituciones.
econ.history-thought.colombian-economy.e.author: author-econ-metrics-1
econ.history-thought.colombian-economy.e.body:
El 10 de marzo de 1923 llegó a Bogotá Edwin Walter Kemmerer, profesor de Princeton y "money doctor" de oficio: iba de país en país ordenando finanzas públicas por encargo de gobiernos que querían verse confiables ante los bancos de Nueva York.

El momento no era casual. Colombia empezaba a recibir los 25 millones de dólares que Estados Unidos pagó por Panamá bajo el tratado Urrutia-Thomson, plata que la prensa bautizó "la danza de los millones", y no existía ninguna institución capaz de administrar semejante entrada. La banca era un conjunto de emisores privados y el gobierno de Pedro Nel Ospina contrató la misión.

De ese trabajo salieron, en cuestión de meses, tres instituciones que siguen en pie: el Banco de la República, la Contraloría General de la República y la Superintendencia Bancaria.

Lo que vale la pena pensar es la paradoja: la entidad más independiente del Estado colombiano nació de una consultoría extranjera contratada, en parte, para tranquilizar a los acreedores. Las instituciones no siempre nacen de las buenas intenciones; a veces nacen de la necesidad de que alguien más te crea.

recall.question: ¿Qué problema concreto vino a resolver la misión Kemmerer en 1923?
recall.answer: Colombia no tenía banco central ni control fiscal moderno justo cuando entraban los 25 millones de dólares de la indemnización por Panamá. La misión creó el Banco de la República, la Contraloría y la Superintendencia Bancaria, y de paso le dio al país una señal de solvencia frente a los prestamistas de Nueva York.

econ.history-thought.keynes-hayek.in-the.title: "In the long run we are all dead"
econ.history-thought.keynes-hayek.in-the.hook: The most quoted line in economics is usually deployed to mean the opposite of what Keynes was saying.
econ.history-thought.keynes-hayek.in-the.author: author-econ-metrics-1
econ.history-thought.keynes-hayek.in-the.body:
From *A Tract on Monetary Reform*, 1923: "But this long run is a misleading guide to current affairs. In the long run we are all dead. Economists set themselves too easy, too useless a task if in tempestuous seasons they can only tell us that when the storm is long past the ocean is flat again."

He was attacking one complacency: the assurance that money is neutral eventually. Quoted today as a licence for short-termism, which reverses him — his complaint was about economists who say nothing useful about the storm.

econ.history-thought.latin-american-stru.title: Prebisch, o por qué exportar café no alcanzaba
econ.history-thought.latin-american-stru.hook: Ricardo decía que a cada quien le conviene especializarse. Prebisch miró cien años de precios y dijo: depende de en qué.
econ.history-thought.latin-american-stru.author: author-econ-metrics-1
econ.history-thought.latin-american-stru.body:
La teoría clásica del comercio es tranquilizadora: cada país se especializa en lo que hace relativamente mejor y todos ganan. Argentina vende carne y trigo, Inglaterra vende máquinas, y el intercambio beneficia a ambos.

Raúl Prebisch, que había dirigido el banco central argentino y vivido el derrumbe de los años treinta desde adentro, no le creyó al cuento. En 1949 escribió para la CEPAL —de la que fue secretario ejecutivo entre 1950 y 1963— un documento que Albert Hirschman llamó el "manifiesto latinoamericano": la economía mundial no es un conjunto de socios simétricos, sino un **centro** industrial y una **periferia** primaria, y el precio relativo de lo que vende la periferia tiende a caer.

Si eso es cierto, el mismo comercio que enriquece al centro va drenando ingreso de la periferia, y especializarse en materias primas es condenarse a correr para quedarse quieto. De ahí salió la industrialización por sustitución de importaciones, la política económica de media América Latina durante tres décadas.

La tesis sigue en disputa, y el argumento detrás es más interesante que el eslogan.
econ.history-thought.latin-american-stru.rigor:
La tesis Prebisch–Singer (1950, formulada de forma independiente por Hans Singer) es una afirmación sobre los **términos de intercambio**, $T=P_{\text{primarios}}/P_{\text{manufacturas}}$: en tendencia secular, $T$ cae.

El mecanismo central es la ley de Engel puesta en el comercio. Si la elasticidad ingreso de la demanda de bienes primarios $\eta_P$ es menor que la de manufacturas $\eta_M$, y el ingreso mundial crece a tasa $g$, la demanda relativa crece a

$$(\eta_P-\eta_M)\,g<0,$$

de modo que, con ofertas parecidas, el precio relativo cae. Prebisch añade un segundo canal, asimétrico: en el centro, sindicatos y poder de mercado convierten el aumento de productividad en salarios y utilidades; en la periferia, con oferta ilimitada de trabajo, se convierte en precios más bajos. La productividad del sur se le regala al norte.

La evidencia empírica es genuinamente discutida: la tendencia estimada depende del periodo, del índice y del tratamiento de la calidad de las manufacturas, y hay quiebres fuertes (los años setenta, el auge de China). La ISI, por su parte, produjo crecimiento industrial en los cincuenta y sesenta y una crisis de deuda en los ochenta.

recall.question: ¿Cuál es el argumento central de la tesis Prebisch–Singer?

options.text: Que la demanda de manufacturas crece más rápido con el ingreso que la de materias primas, de modo que el precio relativo de las segundas tiende a caer.
options.why: es un argumento sobre elasticidades ingreso, no sobre injusticia en sí.

options.text: Que los países ricos imponen aranceles a las materias primas.
options.why: la protección existe, pero el mecanismo de la tesis opera aun con libre comercio.

options.text: Que las materias primas se agotan y por eso suben de precio.
options.why: eso predice lo contrario de lo que afirma la tesis.

options.text: Que la periferia produce con menor productividad que el centro.
options.why: el argumento es sobre quién se queda con las ganancias de productividad, no sobre el nivel.

sources.title: Raúl Prebisch — la CEPAL, el documento de 1949 y la UNCTAD

econ.history-thought.marginal-revolution.title: Three men, three countries, one idea, three years
econ.history-thought.marginal-revolution.hook: In 1871 two men who had never heard of each other published the same idea in London and Vienna. A third followed in Lausanne.
econ.history-thought.marginal-revolution.author: author-econ-metrics-1
econ.history-thought.marginal-revolution.body:
Classical economics could not explain why water is nearly free and diamonds are not. Water is essential; diamonds are decoration. If value came from usefulness, the prices should be reversed — and if it came from labour, as Smith and Ricardo held, you had to explain why so much labour goes into something so useless.

In 1871 William Stanley Jevons published *The Theory of Political Economy* in England, and Carl Menger published his *Grundsätze* in Vienna. Neither knew of the other. Léon Walras, in Lausanne, published his *Éléments* in 1874. All three said the same thing: stop asking what a good is worth in general, and ask what *one more unit* is worth to someone who already has some.

You have plenty of water, so the next litre does almost nothing. You have no diamonds, so the first one does a great deal. Value is about the margin, and the margin is a derivative — which is how economics became a subject with calculus in it.

Hermann Heinrich Gossen had published the same insight in 1854, to an audience of almost nobody. Jevons found out later and admitted the priority in print.

recall.question: How does marginal thinking dissolve the diamond–water paradox?
recall.answer: By separating total usefulness from the value of one more unit. Water's total usefulness is enormous, but it is abundant, so the *marginal* litre is worth almost nothing — and price is set at the margin, not by the total.

sources.title: Marginal revolution — Jevons, Menger and Walras
William Stanley Jevons — The Theory of Political Economy (1871)
Hermann Heinrich Gossen — the 1854 precursor Jevons later acknowledged

econ.history-thought.marx.marx-was-a-ric.title: Marx was a Ricardian, and the arithmetic caught up with him
econ.history-thought.marx.marx-was-a-ric.hook: Marx's economics starts from Ricardo's, taken seriously. The place it broke is an arithmetic problem that took a century to settle.
econ.history-thought.marx.marx-was-a-ric.author: author-econ-metrics-1
econ.history-thought.marx.marx-was-a-ric.body:
Strip away the politics and volume one of *Capital* (1867) is classical economics done stubbornly. Ricardo had said that the value of a commodity traces back to the labour needed to produce it. Marx accepted that and asked where profit comes from if everything exchanges at its value — answering that labour power itself is a commodity, bought at its cost of reproduction, whose use yields more value than it costs.

Then the bill arrives. Industries use very different mixtures of machinery and workers, so if goods sold at their labour values, capital-heavy industries would earn lower profit rates than labour-heavy ones. Competition does not allow that. Volume three, which Engels assembled after Marx's death and published in 1894, tries to convert values into "prices of production" with an economy-wide profit rate — and the conversion does not close.

Böhm-Bawerk pounced in 1896. Bortkiewicz produced a consistent version in 1907, at the cost of Marx's two aggregate equalities. Nobuo Okishio then proved in 1961 that cost-reducing technical change with constant real wages *cannot* lower the profit rate — contradicting one of Marx's central predictions.
econ.history-thought.marx.marx-was-a-ric.rigor:
In volume one a commodity's value is $c+v+s$: constant capital consumed, variable capital (wages), and surplus value. The rate of exploitation is $s/v$ and the profit rate is

$$r=\frac{s}{c+v}=\frac{s/v}{(c/v)+1},$$

falling in the organic composition $c/v$. That is the mechanism behind the predicted tendency of the profit rate to fall.

The **transformation problem** is that competition equalises $r$ across sectors, so sector prices must be $(c+v)(1+r)$ rather than $c+v+s$. Marx transformed outputs at these prices while leaving inputs valued at labour values, which is inconsistent; done simultaneously, Bortkiewicz showed you generally cannot have both "total price = total value" and "total profit = total surplus value".

**Okishio's theorem** closes the other flank. If a technique is adopted because it cuts cost at current prices, and the real wage bundle is unchanged, the new uniform profit rate is at least as high as the old. A falling profit rate therefore needs rising real wages, not mechanisation — a result proved with the same linear-algebra machinery as Sraffa's price systems.

recall.question: What is the transformation problem?

options.text: Prices that equalise profit rates across industries cannot generally be derived from labour values while preserving Marx's aggregate equalities.
options.why: inputs and outputs must be transformed together, and then the totals stop matching.

options.text: That labour cannot be measured in homogeneous units.
options.why: a separate difficulty about reducing skilled to unskilled labour.

options.text: That Marx never finished volume three of Capital.
options.why: Engels did assemble it posthumously, but the inconsistency is mathematical, not editorial.

options.text: That profit rates differ across countries.
options.why: the problem concerns industries within one economy facing a common rate.

econ.history-thought.nobel-stories.the-e.title: The economics Nobel is not one of the Nobels
econ.history-thought.nobel-stories.the-e.hook: It was funded by a central bank for its own 300th birthday, seventy years after Alfred Nobel died.
econ.history-thought.nobel-stories.the-e.author: author-econ-metrics-1
econ.history-thought.nobel-stories.the-e.body:
Alfred Nobel's will named five prizes, and economics was not among them. The Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel was created in 1968, funded by Sweden's central bank on its 300th anniversary, and first awarded in 1969 to Ragnar Frisch and Jan Tinbergen for econometric modelling.

A member of the Nobel family has publicly called it a public-relations coup by economists. The first woman to win it, in 2009, was Elinor Ostrom — a political scientist.

recall.question: Why does the distinction matter beyond pedantry?
recall.answer: Because the prize's prestige is borrowed, and it has shaped which questions count as central economics. Ostrom's win is the counterexample worth remembering: the work that took the prize in 2009 was fieldwork on how communities govern shared resources, done outside the discipline's own methods.

sources.title: Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences

econ.history-thought.smith-ricardo.an-in.title: An invisible hand, twice, and never "the"
econ.history-thought.smith-ricardo.an-in.hook: The most famous metaphor in economics appears twice in everything Adam Smith published, and never with the word 'the'.
econ.history-thought.smith-ricardo.an-in.author: author-econ-metrics-1
econ.history-thought.smith-ricardo.an-in.body:
Adam Smith used the phrase twice in the two books he published: once in *The Theory of Moral Sentiments* (1759), about a landlord whose spending feeds the people who work for him, and once in *The Wealth of Nations* (1776), in a passage arguing that merchants prefer to invest at home.

Both times he wrote "an invisible hand", never "the invisible hand", and never as the name of a principle. The capital-letter doctrine was assembled by twentieth-century economists, Samuelson prominently among them.

recall.question: What is Smith actually arguing in the Wealth of Nations passage?
recall.answer: Something narrow: that merchants, from a preference for investing near home, end up supporting domestic industry without intending to. It is one example of unintended consequences, not a general theorem that self-interest produces the best outcome — the general claim came much later, and the theorem version is the first welfare theorem.

sources.title: Invisible hand — the two occurrences and their later reinterpretation

econ.macro.central-banks.por-que-el-banc.title: Por qué el Banco de la República no le contesta al presidente
econ.macro.central-banks.por-que-el-banc.hook: La Constitución de 1991 dice que el banco central no le presta plata al gobierno salvo por unanimidad. Esa frase tiene teoría detrás.
econ.macro.central-banks.por-que-el-banc.author: author-econ-metrics-1
econ.macro.central-banks.por-que-el-banc.body:
La Constitución de 1991 hizo algo poco romántico y muy efectivo: les quitó a los políticos la máquina de imprimir. Los artículos 371 a 373 crearon un banco central con autonomía, una junta directiva que es la máxima autoridad monetaria, cambiaria y crediticia, y un mandato explícito —mantener la capacidad adquisitiva de la moneda—. Financiar al gobierno requiere el voto unánime de esa junta.

La razón no es que los políticos sean malos, sino que el problema es de incentivos. A cualquier gobierno le conviene prometer inflación baja y luego, una vez firmados los contratos y los salarios, dar un empujón monetario para ganar algo de empleo. Como todo el mundo sabe que le conviene, nadie le cree: los salarios se negocian con la inflación esperada incorporada y el país termina con inflación alta y el mismo empleo de antes. Kydland y Prescott le pusieron nombre en 1977: inconsistencia temporal.

La solución es institucional. Si quien decide no gana elecciones, la promesa se vuelve creíble. La inflación colombiana pasó de niveles de dos dígitos a comienzos de los noventa a un dígito desde finales de la década.
econ.macro.central-banks.por-que-el-banc.rigor:
Tómese una curva de Phillips aumentada por expectativas, $u=u_n-a(\pi-\pi^e)$, y un gobierno que minimiza

$$L=(u-ku_n)^2+\theta\pi^2,\qquad 0<k<1,$$

es decir, que quiere desempleo por debajo del natural. Bajo **discreción**, el gobierno elige $\pi$ tomando $\pi^e$ como dado; la condición de primer orden da $\pi>0$. Pero en equilibrio los agentes no se dejan sorprender de forma sistemática: $\pi^e=\pi$, y entonces $u=u_n$.

Resultado: inflación positiva y ningún empleo adicional. Bajo **regla** —un banco que simplemente anuncia y cumple $\pi=0$— se obtiene el mismo desempleo con inflación cero. La regla domina, y aun así no es un equilibrio si quien manda puede cambiar de opinión mañana.

De ahí el diseño: la independencia no es una opinión sobre la bondad de los banqueros, es un mecanismo de compromiso. Y por eso tiene su propia tensión democrática — una autoridad con enorme poder distributivo y sin urnas encima.

recall.question: ¿Cuál es el argumento económico para que el banco central sea independiente?

options.text: Sin compromiso, el gobierno siempre tiene incentivo a sorprender con inflación, y como todos lo anticipan el resultado es inflación alta sin ganancia de empleo.
options.why: la independencia hace creíble la promesa.

options.text: Porque los tecnócratas entienden la economía mejor que los políticos.
options.why: el argumento no depende de quién sea más competente, sino de quién puede comprometerse.

options.text: Porque así se elimina el desempleo de largo plazo.
options.why: el desempleo de largo plazo no depende de la política monetaria en este modelo.

options.text: Porque impide que el banco central pierda dinero.
options.why: la solvencia del banco no es el problema que motiva el diseño.

sources.title: Banco de la República (Colombia) — autonomía, Junta Directiva y Ley 31 de 1992
Rules Rather than Discretion: The Inconsistency of Optimal Plans
sources.author: Finn E. Kydland & Edward C. Prescott

econ.macro.development.mortality-tables-.title: Eighteenth-century death rates, used to explain today's GDP
econ.macro.development.mortality-tables-.hook: Where European settlers died they built extractive states; where they survived, institutions. That claim became an instrument.
econ.macro.development.mortality-tables-.author: author-econ-metrics-1

reviewed.notes: Softened an unverifiable most-cited-paper superlative.

econ.macro.development.mortality-tables-.body:
Rich countries have good institutions. Do the institutions cause the wealth, or does wealth buy better institutions? Regression cannot answer that, and everyone knew it.

Acemoglu, Johnson and Robinson's 2001 answer was to look for something that moved institutions centuries ago and has no other business in today's income. Their candidate: how dangerous a colony was to Europeans. Where settlers died of malaria and yellow fever, colonisers built extractive machinery to pump out resources with as few Europeans as possible. Where they survived, they built the institutions of home — property rights, courts, representation. Those arrangements persisted long after the diseases were controlled.

Run mortality as an instrument for institutions today and the estimated effect on income is large — larger than the raw regression. It became one of the most cited empirical papers in development economics and part of the 2024 Nobel citation.

It has also been fought over harder than almost any result in economics, and the fight is instructive rather than embarrassing.
econ.macro.development.mortality-tables-.rigor:
The system is

$$\log y_i=\alpha+\beta\,\text{Inst}_i+\varepsilon_i,\qquad \text{Inst}_i=\gamma+\delta\,\log M_i+u_i,$$

with $M_i$ settler mortality. Identification needs relevance ($\delta\neq0$, comfortably satisfied) and exclusion: $\log M_i$ affects income today *only* through institutions.

David Albouy's 2012 comment attacks the data rather than the story: he argues that a majority of the countries have mortality rates imputed from other countries, and that rates for soldiers on campaign, bishops and labourers were pooled in ways that favour the hypothesis. Rebuilding the series with those cases handled differently, the first stage weakens and the IV confidence intervals blow up. Acemoglu, Johnson and Robinson replied in the same issue defending the sources.

The deeper worry is the exclusion restriction, which no data can test: the disease environment plausibly affects productivity, human capital and population density directly. Note also the tell — IV exceeding OLS is often read as evidence of attenuation in the institutions measure, but a violated exclusion restriction produces exactly the same pattern.

recall.question: What is the untestable assumption behind using settler mortality as an instrument?

options.text: That past mortality influences income today only through the institutions colonisers built
options.why: no direct channel through disease, geography or human capital. — exclusion is an argument about the world, never a test on the data.

options.text: That settler mortality is uncorrelated with today's institutions.
options.why: the opposite is required: the instrument must move the endogenous variable.

options.text: That the mortality data were recorded accurately.
options.why: a serious problem raised by Albouy, but one that can be checked against sources.

options.text: That institutions are measured without error.
options.why: measurement error is what IV is partly meant to fix, not an identifying assumption.

econ.macro.financial-crises.a-bank-run-i.title: A bank run is an equilibrium, not a panic
econ.macro.financial-crises.a-bank-run-i.hook: Queueing at a bank you believe is solvent is the rational move, provided you think everyone else will queue too.
econ.macro.financial-crises.a-bank-run-i.author: author-econ-metrics-1
econ.macro.financial-crises.a-bank-run-i.body:
The word "panic" does a lot of dishonest work. It suggests the depositors queueing around the block have lost their heads, and that with better information they would go home.

Diamond and Dybvig showed in 1983 that they are behaving perfectly sensibly. A bank exists to do something genuinely useful: people want their money available at any moment, while the projects worth financing take years. The bank bridges that gap by holding illiquid assets against demandable deposits, which is the service, not a flaw.

But it means the bank can never pay everybody at once. If you believe others will withdraw, the bank must dump its long assets at a loss, and the people at the back of the queue get nothing. So withdrawing is your best response. If you believe nobody will withdraw, waiting pays more and you stay home. Two beliefs, two equilibria, the same balance sheet, no new information required.

The cure follows from the diagnosis: promise to pay everyone regardless. Deposit insurance works by deleting the bad equilibrium, so in the good one it never pays out — and the bill arrives later, as moral hazard.
econ.macro.financial-crises.a-bank-run-i.rigor:
Three dates $t=0,1,2$, a unit endowment, and a technology returning $1$ if liquidated at $t=1$ and $R>1$ at $t=2$. A fraction $\pi$ of depositors turn out to be "early" types who must consume at $t=1$; nobody knows who in advance. Risk-averse agents want insurance against that shock.

The bank offers a demand deposit paying $c_1>1$ at $t=1$ or $c_2<R$ at $t=2$, which beats autarky because it transfers consumption to the early types. Withdrawals are met under a **sequential service constraint**: first come, first served, until the assets run out.

Now the game among late types. If all late types wait, each receives $c_2>c_1$: waiting is optimal. If all late types withdraw, the bank liquidates everything, has $1$ per depositor and pays $c_1>1$ to the first $1/c_1$ of the queue and zero to the rest; expected payoff from waiting is zero, so running is optimal.

Both are Nash equilibria, and nothing distinguishes them but expectations. Deposit insurance changes the payoff to waiting so the run stops being a best response — which is why the guarantee is credible without ever being used.

recall.question: In the Diamond–Dybvig model, what triggers the bad equilibrium?

options.text: Nothing observable needs to change
options.why: it is a shift in what depositors expect other depositors to do. — both outcomes are equilibria of the same game with the same balance sheet.

options.text: The bank's assets turn out to be worth less than its deposits.
options.why: that is insolvency, a different problem; the run happens to a solvent bank.

options.text: Depositors misunderstand the bank's accounts.
options.why: they are fully rational and correctly informed in the model.

options.text: The central bank raises interest rates.
options.why: no monetary policy appears anywhere in the model.

sources.title: Bank Runs, Deposit Insurance, and Liquidity
sources.author: Douglas W. Diamond & Philip H. Dybvig

econ.macro.fiscal-debt.the-only-subtract.title: Whether the debt explodes is one subtraction
econ.macro.fiscal-debt.the-only-subtract.hook: Whether a public debt explodes or melts comes down to one subtraction, and the debt level is not in it.
econ.macro.fiscal-debt.the-only-subtract.author: author-econ-metrics-1
econ.macro.fiscal-debt.the-only-subtract.body:
"Is 60% of GDP too much debt?" is not an answerable question, and the reason is arithmetic rather than politics. What decides whether a debt ratio drifts up or down is the gap between the interest rate the government pays and the growth rate of the economy.

If the economy grows faster than the debt accrues interest, the denominator outruns the numerator. The ratio falls by itself, and a government can run a permanent primary deficit forever without the debt ratio exploding — it converges to a finite level. Olivier Blanchard built his 2019 presidential address to the American Economic Association on the observation that for most of the postwar period, the US paid less on its debt than its economy grew.

Flip the sign and everything inverts. With the interest rate above growth, you must run a primary *surplus* just to keep still, and the required surplus grows with the debt you already have.

That is why emerging-market debt is a different animal. The gap is no constant of nature: it depends on what investors think of you, which depends on the debt — a feedback loop, not a formula.
econ.macro.fiscal-debt.the-only-subtract.rigor:
Let $b$ be debt as a share of GDP, $r$ the real interest rate on debt, $g$ real growth, and $s$ the primary balance (surplus positive) as a share of GDP. In continuous time,

$$\dot b=(r-g)\,b-s .$$

If $r<g$ the coefficient on $b$ is negative and the dynamics are stable: with a permanent primary *deficit* $s<0$, the ratio converges to

$$b^{*}=\frac{s}{r-g}=\frac{|s|}{g-r}>0 .$$

A 2% of GDP deficit with $g-r=1$ point settles at 200% of GDP. Unpleasant, but finite.

If $r>g$ the fixed point is unstable: any debt above $b^*$ grows without bound unless the surplus rises. The required stabilising surplus is $s=(r-g)b$ — proportional to the debt, which is why the same gap is survivable at 30% of GDP and lethal at 90%.

The dangerous part is that $r$ is not exogenous. Investors price default risk off $b$ itself, so $r(b)$ can jump, turning a stable configuration into an unstable one overnight — a sudden stop, in the literature's phrase.

recall.question: A country runs a permanent primary deficit of 2% of GDP, with $r-g=-1\%$. What happens to its debt ratio?

options.text: It converges to a finite level
options.why: here about 200% of GDP — because growth erodes the ratio faster than interest builds it. — stability depends on the sign of $r-g$, not on the deficit's existence.

options.text: It rises without bound, since a permanent deficit always means explosive debt.
options.why: only when $r>g$; otherwise the denominator wins.

options.text: It falls to zero, since $r<g$ means debt shrinks.
options.why: debt shrinks relative to GDP only until the deficit's contribution balances it.

options.text: It depends entirely on the starting debt level.
options.why: the starting level sets the path, but the limit is determined by $s$ and $r-g$.

sources.title: Public Debt and Low Interest Rates
sources.author: Olivier Blanchard

econ.macro.gdp-growth.the-man-who-built-.title: The man who built GDP put the warning in the same report
econ.macro.gdp-growth.the-man-who-built-.hook: Congress asked him to invent a number for how the country was doing. He delivered it with a warning attached.
econ.macro.gdp-growth.the-man-who-built-.author: author-econ-metrics-1

reviewed.notes: Kuznets quote restored verbatim: can, therefore, scarcely be inferred ... as defined above.

econ.macro.gdp-growth.the-man-who-built-.body:
In the depths of the Depression, Congress had no idea how bad things were: there was no national income statistic. Simon Kuznets was commissioned to build one, and his 1934 report to the Senate is the ancestor of every GDP figure since.

In it he wrote: "The welfare of a nation can, therefore, scarcely be inferred from a measurement of national income as defined above."

Ninety years of arguments about growth and wellbeing are, in effect, footnotes to a caveat its own author printed on delivery.

econ.macro.inflation-money.el-dolar-que-.title: El dólar que llegó a costar un millón
econ.macro.inflation-money.el-dolar-que-.hook: En agosto de 1985 un dólar costaba un millón de pesos bolivianos. Once días después de un decreto, los precios dejaron de subir.
econ.macro.inflation-money.el-dolar-que-.author: author-econ-metrics-1

reviewed.notes: Opening figures were wrong: 182,8 % is February 1985, not April 1984, and 2.177,2 % is in no Sachs table. Rebuilt on Sachs (1986), added as a source.

econ.macro.inflation-money.el-dolar-que-.body:
En febrero de 1985 los precios en Bolivia subieron 182,8 % en un solo mes. En la primera mitad de ese año la inflación corrió a un ritmo anual de 26.000 %, y para agosto el dólar se conseguía a un millón de pesos bolivianos en el mercado negro. La gente cargaba fajos de billetes en bolsas y los comercios remarcaban dos veces al día.

Una hiperinflación no es un fenómeno monetario misterioso: es un Estado que gasta lo que no recauda y le pide a su banco central que imprima la diferencia. En 1984 el gobierno central boliviano recaudó 2,6 % del PIB y gastó 33 %.

El 29 de agosto de 1985, el gobierno de Víctor Paz Estenssoro expidió el Decreto Supremo 21060: ajuste fiscal, tipo de cambio flotante —una devaluación efectiva del 95 %—, liberación de precios y apertura comercial. Los precios dejaron de subir el 9 de septiembre.

La lección incómoda es esa velocidad. Si un cambio de régimen fiscal mata una hiperinflación en once días, lo que la sostenía no era la inercia de los precios, sino lo que la gente creía sobre quién iba a pagar la cuenta.

recall.question: ¿Por qué una hiperinflación puede terminar en cuestión de semanas?
recall.answer: Porque su combustible son las expectativas sobre el déficit: mientras se espere que el Estado financie el hueco imprimiendo, nadie retiene moneda. Un cambio creíble del régimen fiscal —Bolivia lo hizo sin control de precios ni reforma monetaria— cambia esa expectativa de golpe, y la demanda de dinero vuelve casi de inmediato.

sources.title: The Bolivian Hyperinflation and Stabilization — tablas de inflación mensual y cuentas fiscales
sources.author: Jeffrey Sachs

econ.macro.solow.a-measure-of-our-ignora.title: Solow measured technology by measuring everything else
econ.macro.solow.a-measure-of-our-ignora.hook: Subtract everything you can measure from growth. Whatever is left is technology — and in Solow's numbers, that was seven-eighths of it.
econ.macro.solow.a-measure-of-our-ignora.author: author-econ-metrics-1
econ.macro.solow.a-measure-of-our-ignora.body:
In 1957 Robert Solow did something almost rude in its simplicity. He took US data from 1909 to 1949, worked out how much of the growth in output per hour could be explained by workers getting more capital to work with, and subtracted. Whatever was left he labelled technical change.

The leftover was about seven-eighths of the growth.

That number reorganised the field. If capital accumulation explains only an eighth of why people became richer, then saving harder is not the road to prosperity, and the interesting variable is whatever "technical change" is standing in for. Everything since — human capital, R&D, institutions, misallocation — has been an attempt to open that box.

It also deserves the nickname Moses Abramovitz gave it a year earlier: "a measure of our ignorance". The residual is defined as what your model failed to account for, so it silently collects mismeasured capital, idle factories, changing quality, market power and your own mistakes.

The definition is an accounting identity, and the assumptions hide in how the weights are chosen.
econ.macro.solow.a-measure-of-our-ignora.rigor:
Write $Y=A\,F(K,L)$ with $F$ constant returns to scale. Differentiating logarithmically,

$$\frac{\dot Y}{Y}=\frac{\dot A}{A}+\alpha\frac{\dot K}{K}+(1-\alpha)\frac{\dot L}{L},\qquad \alpha=\frac{\partial F}{\partial K}\frac{K}{Y},$$

so the **Solow residual** is $\dot A/A=\dot Y/Y-\alpha\dot K/K-(1-\alpha)\dot L/L$: measured growth minus the weighted growth of inputs.

The move that makes this operational is replacing the unobservable output elasticity $\alpha$ with the observable **capital share of income**. That substitution is legitimate only if factors are paid their marginal products — competitive markets and constant returns. With markups, the capital share understates $\alpha$ and the residual absorbs the difference.

So the residual is not a measurement of technology; it is a residual. If utilisation falls in a recession while measured capital does not, productivity appears to fall. Hall's later work used exactly this wedge to estimate markups — turning Solow's error term into somebody else's parameter.

recall.question: Why is the Solow residual called "a measure of our ignorance"?

options.text: It is defined as the part of growth left unexplained, so every mismeasurement and omitted factor ends up inside it.
options.why: it is a leftover, not an observation of technology.

options.text: Because technology cannot be measured in principle.
options.why: parts of it can be, by patents, R&D and quality adjustment; the point is what the residual sweeps up.

options.text: Because Solow's data from 1909 to 1949 were unreliable.
options.why: the critique applies to modern data just as much.

options.text: Because it is usually negative, which makes no sense.
options.why: it is typically positive; the problem is what it contains, not its sign.

econ.macro.solow.one-equation-one-arrow.title: Remember phase lines? The whole Solow model is one
econ.macro.solow.one-equation-one-arrow.hook: One state variable, one autonomous equation, one stable fixed point — and out falls a theory of why poor countries catch up.
econ.macro.solow.one-equation-one-arrow.author: author-econ-metrics-1
econ.macro.solow.one-equation-one-arrow.body:
When you studied autonomous first-order equations, the payoff was that you could read off the entire future without solving anything: draw $\dot x$ against $x$, mark where it crosses zero, note the sign on each side, done. Fixed points and arrows.

Macroeconomics' most-taught model is that picture with economic labels. The state is capital per worker. Each period a fixed fraction of output is saved and added to the stock, while depreciation and a growing population dilute it. Two curves: what saving adds, and what is needed just to stand still. They cross once.

Everything famous about the model is a property of that crossing. Start below it and capital per worker rises — poor countries grow faster, *conditional* on heading to the same crossing point. Raise the saving rate and the crossing moves right: you get richer, permanently, but you grow faster only during the transition. And long-run growth per worker cannot come from capital at all, because the arrow always points back to the same place.

Which is why Solow needed the residual.
econ.macro.solow.one-equation-one-arrow.rigor:
With $k=K/L$, saving rate $s$, depreciation $\delta$, labour growth $n$, and $f$ concave with $f(0)=0$ and the Inada conditions:

$$\dot k = s\,f(k)-(n+\delta)\,k .$$

$\dot k>0$ below the crossing and $\dot k<0$ above it, so the steady state $sf(k^*)=(n+\delta)k^*$ is unique and globally stable on $k>0$. The stability calculation is one line: concavity with $f(0)=0$ gives $f'(k^*)<f(k^*)/k^*$, hence

$$\left.\frac{d\dot k}{dk}\right|_{k^*}=s f'(k^*)-(n+\delta)<s\frac{f(k^*)}{k^*}-(n+\delta)=0 .$$

For Cobb–Douglas $f(k)=k^{\alpha}$, $k^*=\big(s/(n+\delta)\big)^{1/(1-\alpha)}$, and consumption per worker is maximised at the **golden rule** $f'(k_{\text{gold}})=n+\delta$ — saving more than that makes you permanently poorer in consumption, which is the model's one genuinely surprising policy statement.

Add labour-augmenting technical progress at rate $g$ and the same phase line runs in effective units, with long-run growth per worker equal to $g$. The arrow never generates growth; it only decides the level.

recall.question: In the Solow model, a country permanently raises its saving rate. What happens to its long-run growth rate of output per worker?

options.text: Unchanged
options.why: it converges to a higher level, growing faster only along the transition. — long-run per-worker growth is set by technical progress, not by saving.

options.text: Permanently higher, since more capital means more output every year.
options.why: diminishing returns make each extra unit of capital add less, until break-even investment eats it all.

options.text: Permanently lower, because consumption falls.
options.why: consumption can fall if saving exceeds the golden rule, but growth is still governed by $g$.

options.text: It grows without bound, since capital accumulates forever.
options.why: that needs non-diminishing returns to capital, which is the endogenous-growth departure.

econ.macro.unemployment-cycles.good-news.title: Good news can push the unemployment rate up
econ.macro.unemployment-cycles.good-news.hook: A recovery can push the unemployment rate up, and it is not a statistical error. It is the definition doing its job.
econ.macro.unemployment-cycles.good-news.author: author-econ-metrics-1

reviewed.notes: Source title corrected to match the article it actually links to.

econ.macro.unemployment-cycles.good-news.body:
To be counted as unemployed you must satisfy two conditions: no job, and actively looking for one. Drop the second and you vanish from the statistic altogether — you are "out of the labour force", indistinguishable on paper from a retiree.

Now run a recovery. Firms start hiring, word gets around, and people who had given up looking begin again. Each one arrives in the statistics as *unemployed*, because looking is what the definition requires. The denominator grows, the numerator grows, and the published rate can rise in the same month that employment rises. Newspapers report a worsening job market on the day the job market improved.

This is why nobody serious watches the unemployment rate alone. The employment-to-population ratio has no such trapdoor, and participation tells you which way the door is swinging.

And in an economy where a large share of work is informal — no contract, no registration, a stall or a motorbike — being "employed" carries much less information than the word suggests, so the same rate can mean very different things in Bogotá and in Berlin.
econ.macro.unemployment-cycles.good-news.rigor:
With $E$ employed and $U$ unemployed, the labour force is $L=E+U$ and the rate is $u=U/L$. Move one discouraged person from outside the labour force into active search:

$$u'=\frac{U+1}{L+1}>\frac{U}{L}=u \iff L>U \iff E>0 .$$

So re-entry raises the measured rate whenever anyone is employed at all. The effect is not small in a recovery, when re-entry can run for months.

For the cyclical part, **Okun's law** ties the rate to output,

$$\Delta u_t \approx -\beta\,(g_t-g^*),$$

with $\beta$ around $0.5$ in postwar US data: two points of growth above trend buys about one point off unemployment. It is an empirical regularity, not a theorem — $\beta$ differs by country and era, and it drifts precisely because participation and hours absorb part of the adjustment.

recall.question: Employment rose 1% last quarter and the unemployment rate also rose. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: Discouraged workers resumed searching, entering the labour force and the unemployment count at the same time.
options.why: the rate mixes a demand story with a participation story.

options.text: The statistics agency made an error; the two cannot both rise.
options.why: they can and often do, because the labour force is not fixed.

options.text: Firms replaced full-time jobs with part-time ones.
options.why: that would change hours, not the count of employed people.

options.text: Inflation rose, shifting the Phillips curve.
options.why: the Phillips curve relates inflation to unemployment; it does not explain this accounting effect.

econ.micro.consumer-choice.the-giffen-go.title: The counterexample every textbook taught and nobody had found
econ.micro.consumer-choice.the-giffen-go.hook: For a century the textbook counterexample to downward-sloping demand had no confirmed example. Then someone ran the experiment in Hunan.
econ.micro.consumer-choice.the-giffen-go.author: author-econ-metrics-1
econ.micro.consumer-choice.the-giffen-go.body:
Demand curves slope down. Every course says so, then immediately mentions the exception — the Giffen good, where a price *rise* makes people buy *more*. For over a century the illustration was Irish potatoes during the famine, and when historians checked the potato data, it did not hold up.

Robert Jensen and Nolan Miller went and made one. In 2006 and 2007 they randomly handed poor households in Hunan vouchers that cut the price of rice, their staple, and did the same for wheat in Gansu. If rice behaves like a Giffen good, cheaper rice should make households buy *less* of it. Among the poor households in Hunan, that is what happened; the wheat evidence in Gansu was weaker.

The mechanism is almost obvious once you see it. If rice is most of your calories and most of your budget, a fall in its price makes you *richer* — and a slightly richer household buys a little meat and slightly less rice. The good has to be near-subsistence for this to bite, which is why nobody ever found it in a rich country.
econ.micro.consumer-choice.the-giffen-go.rigor:
The Slutsky decomposition splits a price change into a substitution effect along an indifference curve and an income effect:

$$\frac{\partial x}{\partial p}=\underbrace{\left.\frac{\partial x}{\partial p}\right|_{u}}_{\le 0}-\;x\,\frac{\partial x}{\partial m}.$$

The first term is always weakly negative — a compensated price rise never raises demand. So a Giffen good requires the second term to dominate, which needs two things at once: the good must be **inferior**, $\partial x/\partial m<0$, and the budget share $x p/m$ must be large, since the income effect scales with $x$.

That combination is exactly a subsistence staple for a poor household, and it explains the failures of earlier hunts. It also explains Jensen and Miller's non-result for the very poorest: households too poor to afford *any* meat have nothing to substitute toward, so the income effect has nowhere to go.

The law of demand survives intact in its honest form: compensated demand slopes down, always. Uncompensated demand is what can misbehave.

recall.question: What does a good need in order to be Giffen?

options.text: To be inferior and to take up a large share of the budget, so the income effect can outweigh the substitution effect.
options.why: that combination points straight at subsistence staples.

options.text: To be a luxury whose appeal rises with its price.
options.why: that is a Veblen good, a different (and demand-shifting) story.

options.text: To have no close substitutes at any price.
options.why: helpful for a strong income effect, but not sufficient on its own.

options.text: To be consumed only by the very poorest households.
options.why: the very poorest showed no Giffen behaviour, because they had nothing to substitute toward.

econ.micro.externalities-public-goods.th.title: The bees had contracts
econ.micro.externalities-public-goods.th.hook: The textbook example of a market failure turned out to have a going rate, printed in a pollination contract, for decades.
econ.micro.externalities-public-goods.th.author: author-econ-metrics-1
econ.micro.externalities-public-goods.th.body:
James Meade built the standard classroom example of an externality in 1952: the apple grower and the beekeeper. Bees pollinate the orchard, blossoms feed the bees, and neither is paid for what they give the other. Nobody can charge a bee. So both do too little, and only a subsidy can fix it. It went into the textbooks.

In 1973 Steven Cheung went to Washington State and read the contracts. Beekeepers and farmers had been trading these services for years, in writing, with prices that moved sensibly: farmers *paid* rental fees for hives on crops that needed pollination, while beekeepers paid the farmer for access to crops that yielded good nectar. There were customary rates, seasonal terms, and enforcement by reputation in a small industry.

The lesson Coase had already argued in 1960: an externality is not a property of a good, it is a symptom of the cost of making a deal. Where the parties are few, identifiable, and dealing repeatedly, the deal gets made.

The honest limit is right there in the conditions. Nobody has yet found the contract between a coal plant and everyone downwind.

recall.question: What does the bee case actually show about externalities?
recall.answer: Not that they are imaginary — that whether one persists depends on transaction costs. Few parties, clear property rights and repeat dealing make private bargains possible; millions of diffuse victims and no assignable rights make them impossible, which is where taxes and regulation earn their place.

econ.micro.firms-costs.every-doubling-ta.title: Cost falls by a fifth every time you double everything you have ever built
econ.micro.firms-costs.every-doubling-ta.hook: Airframe costs in 1936 fell by a fifth every time total production doubled. The same exponent turns up in ships, chips and solar panels.
econ.micro.firms-costs.every-doubling-ta.author: author-econ-metrics-1
econ.micro.firms-costs.every-doubling-ta.body:
In 1936 Theodore Wright looked at aircraft factories and found a pattern that had nothing to do with factory size. Every time *cumulative* production doubled — not output per month, total planes ever built — the labour needed for the next one fell by about twenty percent. Workers learn, tools get jigs, the fiftieth wing is not the fifth wing.

The number kept showing up. Liberty ships in the war, transistors, solar modules, batteries: different industries, progress ratios clustered in the same neighbourhood.

Why it matters is that it makes cost a function of *history*, not of current scale. Two firms with identical factories have different costs if one started earlier. A technology that looks hopelessly expensive today is not expensive because of physics; it is expensive because nobody has built many. And a subsidy that buys quantity can be self-justifying — which is an argument policy makers love, and should be made to prove.

Because proving it is genuinely hard, for a reason you already know.
econ.micro.firms-costs.every-doubling-ta.rigor:
Write $C_x$ for the cost of the $x$-th cumulative unit. Wright's law is a power law,

$$C_x=C_1\,x^{\log_2 b},$$

where $b$ is the **progress ratio**: cost after a doubling relative to cost before. Wright's aircraft gave $b\approx0.8$, so the exponent is $\log_2 0.8\approx-0.32$. On log–log axes it is a straight line, which is why the plots all look so convincing.

Keep it distinct from economies of scale, where cost falls with the *rate* of output at a point in time. Learning depends on accumulated experience; scale on current volume. A firm can have one and not the other.

And here is the econometric catch. Cumulative production grows with time, and so does everything else — general technical progress, input prices, quality. Regressing log cost on log cumulative output attributes all of it to learning, by construction. Separating the two needs variation in production that is not variation in time: a policy shock, a war, a subsidy with a cutoff.

recall.question: A solar-module maker's cost per watt falls 20% every time cumulative output doubles. What does that say about economies of scale?

options.text: Nothing directly
options.why: the learning curve tracks accumulated experience, while scale economies track the current rate of output. — a firm can show one without the other.

options.text: That average cost falls as the plant gets bigger.
options.why: that is the scale story, which this pattern does not measure.

options.text: That marginal cost is below average cost at every output.
options.why: a statement about one moment's cost curve, unrelated to the history of production.

options.text: That the firm has a natural monopoly.
options.why: steep learning can favour incumbents, but it is not the natural-monopoly condition.
